New York City, located in the + 5 or R zone,
observes Eastern Standard Time (EST). When it is 5:00
p.m. EST in New York, it is 10:00 p.m. GMT in
Greenwich (standard clock time in New York plus the
zone number in hours: 5:00 p.m. EST + 5:00 = 10:00
p.m. GMT.
The Standard Time Meridian for Berlin, Germany
is 15° E 00'. This is the -1 or A zone. When it is 5:00
p.m. standard time in Berlin, it is 4:00 p.m. in
Greenwich (5:00 p.m. - 1:00 = 4:00 p.m. GMT).
Places that observe or have observed Daylight
Savings Time, War Time or Double Summer Time
(Great Britain) are listed in the time zone/time changes
books with appropriate dates. If a birth is recorded
in Daylight Savings Time or War Time, the time must
be changed to standard time by subtracting one hour
from clock time before converting to Greenwich Mean
Time. Two hours are subtracted from Double Summer
Time in order to obtain standard time.
To convert 10:00 a.m. EasternDaylightTime(EDT)
to GMT these two steps are followed:
(1) 10:00 a.m. EDT - 1:00 = 9:00 A.M. EST
(Daylight Savings Time minus one hour equals
standard time.) Eastern Standard Time is in the
+ 5 zone.
(2) 9:00 a.M. EST + 5:00 = 2:00 P.M. GMT
(Standard clock time plus zone number in hours
equals GMT.)
All localities do not use standard time. Places that
observe Local Mean Time (True Local Time) are listed
in the time zone books along with local time
information. The calculation required to convert Local
Mean Time (LMT) to Greenwich Mean Time is given
in Chapter 12
Astrological data is based on sidereal time (star
time). Sidereal time, measured in relation to fixed
stars, differs from Sun time (solar time), on which
most clocks are based, by about four minutes each
day. A sidereal day is made up of twenty-three hours,
fifty-six minutes and four seconds of clock time: a solar
day (clock day) contains twenty-four hours, three
minutes and fifty-six seconds of sidereal time. The
difference amounts to 9.8(3 seconds per hour.
Tables of Houses
A Table of Houses lists the position of the MC
(Midheaven) tor the sidereal times at which it moves
ahead 1° in the zodiac, it advances 1° in approximatelv

=== Page 106 ===
122 Compendium of Astrology
four minutes of sidereal time. The positions of the
Ascendant and other house cusps at those particular
times are given for various degrees of north latitude. This
data is adapted to birth localities in south latitude by a
simple computation, which is shown in Chapter 12.
Tables of Houses vary according to the system of
horoscope erection for which they are designed. There
is some disagreement among astrologers as to which
house system yields the most accurate interpretation,
for planets and signs do not always occupy the same
houses in different systems. Most astrologers study
several systems until they determine the one which
seems, to them, valid.
The Equal House system, one of the oldest, is based
on equal divisions of the ecliptic. In this system all
house cusps bear the same numerical degree as the
Ascendant; the signs on the cusps follow the natural
order of the zodiac beginning with the sign dn the
Ascendant. Each house contains 30°; there are no
intercepted signs. The MC is inserted in the horoscope
at the proper zodiacal degree (Figure 15).
The Placidean system, designed by the Italian monk
Placidus de Tito in the seventeenth century, is
currently the most widely used quadrant system
(unequal house) of horoscope erection. In this system
time is adapted to space. House cusps are calculated
from two trisected semi-arcs, the time in right
ascension (sidereal time expressed in degrees and
minutes of arc) it takes for each degree of the ecliptic
to rise from the lower meridian to the horizon
(nocturnal semi-arc) and the time to rise from the
horizon to the upper meridian (diurnal semi-arc). This
system breaks down at latitudes greater than 66° 33'
because some degrees are circumpolar (do not touch
the horizon near the poles) and form only diurnal or
nocturnal semi-arcs, not both, in far northern or
southern locations.
A comparatively new system, the Koch or
Birthplace house system, devised several years ago
by Dr. Walter Koch, is rapidly becoming popular. In
this method, based on time dynamics, the position of
each degree of the ecliptic is considered relative to the
Ascendant and the birthplace. The polar elevation
of the birthplace is included in calculations for all
house cusps.
Two other quadrant house systems, Campanus
(thirteenth century) and Regiomontanus (fifteenth
century), both space systems, are still much in use.
In space systems, a reference great circle is divided into
twelve sections; other great circles that pass through
the points of division, the ecliptic and the north and
south points of the horizon are calculated. House cusps
are found at the points of intersection of these circles
and the ecliptic. The Campanus system is based on
division of the prime vertical, the great circle that rises
vertically and passes through Earth's zenith, nadir, and
east point of the-horizon; the Regiomontanus method
uses Earth's equator as its reference great circle.
Another system favored by many. Porphyry (third
century), combines equal house and quadrant
methods. Each quadrant of the horoscope as
determined by the Ascendant and MC and their
opposite points, the Descendant and IC, are divided
into three houses of equal size. Houses in the first
and third quadrants contain the same number of
degrees; houses in the second and fourth quadrant are
alike in size.
The method of horoscope calculation and
construction is the same for all house systems; the
difference lies in the data given in theTable of Houses
for each system.
In order to use a Table of Houses one must first
calculate the Local Sidereal Time. The Local Sidereal
Time is the sidereal time that corresponds to clock time
at the time and place of birth.
The calculated Local Sidereal Time is found in
the Table of Houses. The MC and Ascendant listed
for that time at the latitude of the birthplace are
entered in the horoscope blank. For systems other than
Equal House, the intermediate house cusps that
correspond to the Local Sidereal Time and birth
latitude are also entered.
The MC forms the cusp of the tenth house in all
quadrant systems. The opposite point in the zodiac
is the cusp of the fourth house. This is the IC. The
fourth house falls opposite the tenth in the horoscope.
In the Equal House system, the MC is not the cusp
of the tenth house nor is the IC the cusp of the
fourth house.
Tables of Houses list only the cusps for six houses:
1 (Ascendant), 2, 3, 10 (MC), 11 and 12. The
remaining six houses bear the same degree and
opposite sign as the house opposed in the horoscope.

Each of the six large columns shown in Figure 13
contains five subcolumns headed 11, 12, 1, 2 and 3.
The subcolumn headed "1" lists the degrees and
minutes of the Ascendant, which is the cusp of the first
house. The other subcolumns list the degrees and
tenths of a degree of the house cusp that corresponds
to the heading number. The numerical value of the
digit representing tenths of a degree is multiplied by
6 to obtain minutes of arc (ignore the decimal point).
The degrees and decimal point are not repeated for
each column entry. If no degree is listed one must look
up the column to the previous degree entry. Do not
omit degrees; if a house cusp is placed at 0°, a zero
will be indicated in the column.
The appropriate sign for each house cusp is entered
directly below th^ heading number. Sign changes
that occur at various latitudes are listed throughout
the column.
In Figure 13 find the sidereal time 20:12:54 at the top
of the page in the fifth column. The MC is listed beside
the sidereal time. At this time the MC is 1° Aquarius.
Find 41° in the latitude column; go across the row
to the large column headed 20:12:54. Look under the
corresponding subcolumn headed "1" in the 41° row
to find the zodiacal longitude of the Ascendant for a
birth that took place at 41° north latitude and occurred
at 20:12:54 Local Sidereal Time. The sign of the
Ascendant is at the top of that subcolumn directly
beneath the heading number "1." The Ascendant for
41° north latitude at 20:12:54 Local Sidereal Time is
22026' Taurus. This is the zodiacal position of the cusp
of the first house.
The cusp of the seventh house (Descendant) lies
directly opposite the Ascendant in the horoscope. In
this example, the zodiacal position of the Descendant
is22026' Scorpio, the point opposite 22026' Taurus
(the Ascendant) in the zodiac.
To determine the remaining Placidean house cusps
for this same sidereal time and latitude, find the cusps
for 2, 3, 11 and 12 in the 41° row under the large
column headed 20:12:54 in Figure 13. Reverse these
cusp positions for houses 8, 9, 5 and 6. The Placidean
house cusps for this horoscope are shown in Figure
14. (Note that neither Virgo nor Pisces appears on a
house cusp. These signs are enclosed in parentheses
to indicate interception. Virgo is intercepted in the fifth
house; Pisces is intercepted in the eleventh.)

Ephemerides
An ephemeris lists the zodiacal positions and decli-
nations of the planets and Moon's North Node at the
given sidereal time at Greenwich for a specified clock
time each day. The data in a noon ephemeris is correct
at 12.00 noon GMT (12:00 p.m.). Data in a zero hour
(midnight) ephemeris is correct at 12:00 midnight
GMT (12:00 a.m. = 00:00:00). Ephemerides are
printed in editions that cover from one to two
thousand years. Planetary data listed for a birthdate
of interest must be corrected according to time of birth.

The month and year appear above the columns; the
first column, headed "DAY," lists the date and
weekday and the second gives the ephemeris sidereal
time at Noon GMT on the corresponding date. The
listed sidereal time must be adjusted according to
birthtime and birthplace. Entries for the zodiacal
positions of the planets and the Moon's North Node
follow across the page in the upper section of the table
marked "LONGITUDE at NOON" in columns headed
by their symbols (glyphs). Zodiacal longitude is listed
to the nearest tenth of a minute of arc, each tenth being
equal to six seconds of arc. When inserting planets in
a horoscope, it is customary to round off the positions
to the nearest minute.
The glyph for the sign each planet occupies is
entered in the ephemeris for the first day of the month.
If a planet changes sign during the course of a month,
the sign change is noted at Noon GMT on the
appropriate date. Figure 16 shows that the Sun (third
column) is in Scorpio on the first day of November
1950. Note the similarity between the glyph for
Scorpio and for Virgo, which appears under Saturn,
and learn to distinguish between the two. The glyph
for Virgo always has a cross stroke on the last leg of
the "m"; sometimes the glyph for Scorpio has an
arrowhead pointing upward on the last stroke. Refer
to pictures of glyphs in Chapter 2 in the Virgo and
Scorpio sections.
In the column for the Sun, notice that it had entered
Sagittarius on November 23. Four other planets also
change sign once in November; Mercury from Scorpio
to Sagittarius on the 15th (sixth column), Venus from
Scorpio to Sagittarius on the 21st (seventh column).
Mars from Sagittarius to Capricorn on the 6th (eighth
column), and Saturn from Virgo to Libra on the 21st
(tenthcolumn). The column for the Moon (fifth) shows
that this fast-moving planet changes sign every two
and one-half days.
Notice the eleventh column, headed Uranus. An "R"
is inserted between the degrees and minutes of
longitude on November 2. The "R" means that Uranus
is retrograde. The retrograde symbol is not repeated
each day; it is entered only on the day a planet goes
retrograde and on the second day of each month
thereafter that the planet remains retrograde (some
ephemerides note retrograde motion on the first day
of the month). Note that Pluto (last column) goes
retrograde on the 24th. A planet is retrograde from
the date the "R" is first entered until the date on which
a "D" is entered to signify direct motion. Direct motion
is not indicated in the ephemeris except on the date
of transition from retrograde to direct motion. Always
check the planet columns from the birthdate upward
for a change in motion or sign.
To denote retrograde motion in a horoscope, an "R"
is written beside the planet's position. Direct motion
is not indicated in a horoscope unless a planet goes
direct on the GMT birthdate.
Some ephemerides list the stationary periods of
planetary motion; most do not. In order to estimate
the stationary period, note a planet's zodiacal position
on the transition date; that is, the date that a planet
changes motion from direct to retrograde (the date on
which an "R" is first entered during a retrograde
period) or from retrograde to direct as indicated by
a "D." A planet is stationary on those consecutive days
immediately preceding and/or following the transition
date for which the zodiacal longitude is the same as
on the transition date. No variation of position is
allowed, as even a change in seconds of arc indicates
some motion. A planet is stationary on the transition
date but may remain so for only a brief time.
An "S" is used to distinguish a stationary planet in a
horoscope. If a birth occurs on the transition date, a
stationary planet is marked "SD" or "SR" to indicate
stationary direct or stationary retrograde, asapplicable.
In Figure 16, the distance in arc that a planet lies
north or south of the celestial equator, its declination,
is listed for every third day in the lower columns for
November 1950. Direction of declination (N = north;
S = south) is indicated in the first entry and through-
out the column as changes occur. Declinations, exact
at Noon GMT on the entry date, are corrected
according to birthdate and birthtime.

Calculation of House Cusps
The first step in determining the house cusps for a
horoscope is the calculation of the Local Sidereal Time
(LST) at birth. One must be able to perform various
mathematical operations involving time and longitude
in order to calculate the Local Sidereal Time.
Mathematical Operations
Longitude
In mathematical operations involving longitude, the
units are dealt with separately. Degrees may be
converted to minutes of arc and minutes converted
to seconds of arc if necessary to complete calcula-
tions. Conversions are based on the following
longitude equivalents:
1 degree = 60 minutes of arc
1 minute of arc = 60 seconds of arc
Subtraction
To subtract 3o50' from 80o15', 80o15' must first be
changed to 79°75' (50' cannot be subtracted from 15')
by converting 80° to 79°60' and adding the 60' to the
15'. The subtraction is carried out as follows:
80°15' _ 79°75'
- 3°50' " - B'SO'
76 °25'
Addition
The minutes and seconds in a longitude sum may be
greater in number than the basic equivalent units. If
a sum has more than 60' or 60", the multiples of 60
are reduced to degrees or minutes respectively. For
example, add 5° 46'18" to 24025'48":
24°25'48"
+ 5°46'18"
29°71'66" = 30°12'6"
In this example the 66" in the initial answer was
reduced to 1' 6", the 1' was added to the 71', giving
72', the 72' was then reduced to 1012', the 1° was
added to the 29° for a final result of 30° 12'6". In
conversions of this kind all degrees, minutes and
seconds must be accounted for.
Time
In computations involving time, the hours, minutes
and seconds are treated as separate units Hours may
be converted to minutes and minutes to seconds or
vice versa. It is correct to add 24 hours in order to
carry out calculations or to subtract 24 hours in order
to reduce the final result to the lowest unit. The
following equivalents are used in time conversions:
1 day - 24 hours
1 hour = 60 minutes of time
1 minute of time = 60 seconds of time
Subtraction
A greater number of hours may be subtracted from
a lesser number of hours by adding 24 hours to the
lesser number. To subtract 10:2415 (ten hours

Sidereal Time Variation
Sidereal time varies from solar time (clock time) by
9.86 seconds per hour. To calculate the sidereal time
variation over a period of time, multiply the time
interval in hours by 9.86; the result is seconds of time.
The sidereal time variation for a period of 3 hours is
calculated thus:
3 hr. X 9.86 sec. per hr. = 29.58 sec. = 30 sec.
(to the nearest second)
In this calculation the " X " indicates multiplication.
The final answer is rounded off to the nearest second.
A decimal remainder of less than .50 (one-half) is
dropped; 1 second is added if the decimal remainder
is equal to or greater than .50 as in the above example.
To calculate the time variation over a period of
minutes, the minutes are written as a fraction of an hour,
and this fraction is multiplied by 9.86. The number of
minutes in the time period forms the numerator of the
fraction (the numerals above or to the left of the
fractional line) and the number of minutes in 1 hour (60)
forms the denominator (the numerals below or to the
right of the fractional line). For example, proceed as
follows to calculate the sidereal time variation for a
period of 3 hours and 15 minutes:
1. Write the ipinutes as a fraction of an hour:
15 min. = "/io hr.
2. Solve the problem as in the previous example:
31%o hr. X 9.86 sec. per hr. = 32.04 sec. = 32 sec.
If a calculator is not available, it is easier to convert
the minutes to a decimal fraction before carrying out
the multiplication. To convert a fraction into decimal
form, divide the numerator by the denominator as
follows:
15/6o = 0.25 (The line dividing the numerator
and denominator of the fraction indicates
division. 'Vso is correctly read as the fraction
"fifteen-sixtieths" or as 15 divided by 60. The
division is simpler to handle if the fraction
is first reduced to the lowest common
denominator: ls/6o = W)
The total time period, 3 hours and 15 minutes, is
written as 3.25 hours and multiplied by 9.86:
3.25 hr. X 9.86 sec. per hr. = 32.04 sec. = 32 sec.
In this example .04 was dropped because it is less
than .50.
A close approximation of the sidereal time variation
is obtained by allowing 10 seconds per hour and 1
second per 6 minutes of clock time; fractions of a
second are dropped from the final answer. To estimate
the time variation, the number of hours is multiplied
by 10, the number of minutes is divided by 6, and the
two results are added together. The final answer is
seconds of time. The time variation for an interval of
3 hours and 15 minutes is estimated as follows:
3 X 10 = 30 sec.
(number of hours of time interval multiplied by 10)

(number of minutes divided by 6, the fractional

Conversion of Standard Time
to Local Mean Time
Some astrological calculations require that a birthtime
recorded in standard time be converted to Local Mean
Time (LMT). Local Mean Time is based on the position
ol the Sun relative to a particular locality. It is 12:00
p.m. (noon) Local Mean Time in a given locality when
the Sun reaches its highest point in the sky relative
to that place. Clocks based on standard time read noon
throughout the entire time zone when the Sun reaches
its high point overhead at the Standard Time

=== Page 114 ===
130 Compendium of Astrology
Meridian. Because the Sun appears to move from east
to west across the sky, the Sun has passed the noon
point in places east of the Standard Time Meridian
before standard time clocks there read noon; the Sun
has not reached the noon point in places west of the
Standard Time Meridian when standard time clocks
in those places read noon.
When standard time clocks read noon in localities
east of the Standard Time Meridian, it is actually
later according to Local Mean Time because the Sun
has already passed the noon point in those places.
When standard time clocks read noon in places west
of the Standard Time Meridian, it is actually earlier
by Local Mean Time because the Sun has not yet
reached the noon point overhead. The time difference
between Local Mean Time and standard time depends
upon the distance in longitude between the birth
locality of interest and the Standard Time Meridian
in use in that locality.
To convert a standard birthtime to Local Mean
Time, the longitude differential (distance in arc
between the longitude of the birthplace and the
longitude of the Standard Time Meridian in use at the
birthplace) is changed to time units. The longitude
differential expressed in units of time is added to the
standard time for birth localities that lie east of the
Standard Time Meridian; the differential is subtracted
from standard time if the birthplace is situated west
of the Standard Time Meridian.
In the following example a 6:30 p.m. EST birthtime
is converted to Local Mean Time. The Standard Time
Meridian for the Eastern Standard Time zone (EST)
is 75° W. The birthplace is located at 73° W 35'.
Step 1. Calculate the longitude differential.
75°WOO' _ 74o60' (longitude of the STM)
- 73° W35' - 73°35' (longitude of the
 _ _ birthplace)
1°25' (longitude differential)
Step 2. Convert the longitude differential into time
units.
1° X 4 = 4 min. = 00:04:00
25' X 4 = lOOsec. = 1 min. and 40sec. = 00:01:40
00:04:00
4-00:01:40
00:05:40 (longitude time differential)
Step 3. Add or subtract ftie longitude time differential
found in Step 2 from the standard time of birth
according to whether the birthplace lies east
or west of the Standard Time Meridian.
6:30:00 p.m. EST (standard time of birth)
+ 00:05:40 (longitude time differential)
6:35:40 p.m. LMT (Local Mean Time at birth)
It is irrelevant to Step 3 whether the brithplace is
located east or west of Greenwich; the location of the
birthplace in reference to the Standard Time Meridian
is the pertinent factor.
The birthplace in the preceding example lies west
of Greenwich (west longitude), but it is located east
of the Standard Time Meridian; therefore, the longi-
tude time differential was added to standard clock time
in order to obtain the corresponding Local Mean Time.
Conversion of Birthtime
to Local Sidereal Time
Before calculations are begun, the name of the subject,
the date of birth, the place of birth, the time of birth
and the kind of clocktime in effect on the birthdate
are recorded. A birthtime given in Daylight Savings
Time or War Time is changed to standard time. The
longitude and latitude of the birthplace are noted.
Printed calculation sheets and horoscope blanks
provide space for such data.
There are several methods of calculating the Local
Sidereal Time. The astrologer uses the method with
which he or she feels at ease. The two most common
methods are presented here. The student should
become familiar with both methods as a check against
errors until the calculations are mastered.
Method I: The LMT Method of Calculation
Until standard time was adopted on a world-wide basis,
many localities observed Local Mean Time. The LMT
method for calculating the Local Sidereal Time of birth
was developed before the adoption of standard time.
In this method, the sidereal time listed in the ephemeris
is adjusted to allow for the time interval between the
Local Mean Time of birth and the ephemeris reference
time. Two corrections are applied to this adjusted
sidereal time to account for the 9.86 seconds per hour
variation between sidereal time and clock time: one
correction is based on the time interval, the other is

Method II: The GMT Method of Calculation
The GMT method of calculating the Local Sidereal
Time has grown in popularity with the increased use
of standard time. In this method the birthtime is first
converted to Greenwich Mean Time. This step serves
a dual purpose; corrections that are applied to planetary
positions listed in the ephemeris also require the
calculation of the Greenwich Mean Time of birth. The
sidereal time listed in the emphemeris on the GMT
birthdate is adjusted according to the GMT birthtime.
The GMT birthdate is the date on which the GMT
birthtime occurs. It is usually the same day as the
recorded birthdate, but it may be the day preceding or
following the given date. One correction applied to the
GMT interval includes the longitude time correction.
The sidereal time adjustment and subsequent correction
give the sidereal time at Greenwich at the time of birth;
the Greenwich sidereal time is then adapted to the
longitude of the birthplace to determine the Local
Sidreal Time at the place of birth.

Correcting the House Cusps
for a Placidean Horoscope
The position of the house cusps for a horoscope may
be taken directly from the Table of Houses if the exact
Local Sidereal Time and latitude of the birthplace are
listed. If the Local Sidereal Time falls between two
consecutive sidereal time listings, the positions of the
house cusps are interpolated according to the
proportional sidereal time difference. Except for the
MC (Midheaven), which forms the cusp of the tenth
house in the Placidean system of horoscope erection,
a similar interpolation is made based on latitude for
births that do not occur at an exact degree of latitude
listed in the Table of Houses.
Time Correction for House Cusps
The position of a house cusp moves in proportion to the
corresponding time change. The ratio of the sidereal time
increment to the sidereal time interval is equal to the ratio
of the house cusp increment to the house cusp interval
at a specified degree of latitude. The sidereal time
increment (ST increment) is the time difference between
the calculated Local Sidereal Time (LST) at birth and the
closest earlier sidereal time listed in the Table of Houses;
the sidereal time interval (ST interval) is the time
difference between the closest earlier sidereal time and
the following (later) consecutive sidereal time listed (the
calculated LST will fall between these two listings); the
house cusp increment is the distance in arc a cusp moves
during the time span of the ST increment; the house cusp
interval is the distance a cusp moves during the ST
interval.
A fractional equation can be formed as follows:
ST increment Cusp increment
ST interval — Cusp interval
The equation can be transposed and written in the
following manner:
ST increment j— X Cusp interval = Cusp increment
This equation describes Vhe mathematical operations
to be performed in order to calculate the house cusp
increment. They are: Divide the ST increment by the ST
interval and multiply the result by the cusp interval. The
final result is the correction (cusp increment) to be
applied to the house cusp position listed at the closest
earliersidereal time to account for the motion of the cusp
during the time span between the closest earlier sidereal
time listed and the calculated Local Sidereal Time at
birth.
The data needed to correct a house cusp for time
include:
(a) the Local Sidereal Time at birth
(b) the closest earlier sidereal time listed
(c) the closest later sidereal time listed
(d) the position of the house cusp of interest at the
closest earlier sidereal time listed for the degree of
birth latitude
(e) the position of the house cusp of interest at the
closest later sidereal time listed for the degree of
birth latitude.

The Use of Logarithms
The calculation in Step 6 is relatively simple with the
use of a calculator; without one the division and
multiplication can be complicated. An alternate
mathematical method, which involves subtraction and
addition instead of division and multiplication, is
frequently employed. In this method proportional
logarithms (logs) replace the original numerical units;
there is no need to convert time or longitude to like
units or smaller units. Logs (numbers), which
correspond to the time and/or longitude (or latitude)
in a particular problem, are found in a proportional
logarithm table (log table). If the original problem
requires division, the log that represents the divisor
is subtracted from the log that replaces the dividend:
if the problem requires multiplication the corre-
sponding logs are added.

(a) Log of ST increment
— Log of ST interval
Log of ST factor
(b) Log of ST factor

Log of cusp increment
The logs in (a) are subtracted because the original
problem called for division of the ST increment
(dividend) by the ST interval (divisor). The logs in (b)
are added because the ST factor is multiplied by the
cusp increment in the original problem. In problems
of this sort, the log of the ST factor is a constant that
is used to correct each house cusp of the horoscope
for time. The log of the cusp interval for each house
cusp is added to the same constant, the log of the ST
factor, to determine the time correction for that cusp.

To Correct the Intermediate
House Cusps for Time
The intermediate house cusps are corrected for time
in the same manner as the Ascendant. Always note
whether a house cusp moves forward or backward in
the zodiac as the sidereal time increases from the earlier
reference ST to the later ST. The cusp correction is
subtracted from the earlier position if the cusp moves
backward (decreases).
Latitude Correction_for House Cusps
All house cusps except the MC must be corrected for
latitude unless the exact latitude of the birthplace is
listed in the Table of Houses. In order to calculate the
correction for latitude, the latitude increment is divided
by the latitude interval, and the result is multiplied
by the distance in arc that the time corrected cusp
moves during the latitude interval. For most Tables
of Houses the latitude interval is 1° (the difference
between the degree of birth latitude and the next higher
degree of latitude listed); the latitude increment equals
the minutes of latitude of the birthplace.
The mathematical operations that yield the cusp
correction for latitude are similar to those used to
determine the time correction for house cusps. The
problem is stated as follows:
Latitude increment X Cusp distance Latitude interval
= Cusp correction for latitude
The data required to correct a house cusp for
latitude include:
(a) the latitude of the birthplace
(b) the next higher degree of latitude listed in
the Table of Houses
(c) the time corrected house cusp for the degree
of latitude at the birthplace
(d) the time corrected house cusp for the next
higher degree of latitude.

Summary of House Cusp Calculation
1. Calculate and record the Local Sidereal Time
that corresponds to the clock time of birth at the place
of birth. Look for the calculated Local Sidereal Time
in a Table of Houses. If the Local Sidereal Time
appears in the table, the MC listed for that time may
be entered on the chart form without correction. The
other house cusps that are listed for this time at the
degree of latitude of birth need only be adjusted to
the exact latitude of the birthplace according to the
procedure outlined in Steps 13-19.
2. If the Local Sidereal Time of birth does not
appear in the Table of Houses, it will fall between two
consecutive sidereal time listings, one that is earlier
in time than the Local Sidereal Time and one that is
later. Record these two sidereal times. Label the earlier
time "earlier ST"; label the later time "later ST."
3. Calculate and record the time difference
between the Local Sidereal Time of birth and the
earlier ST. Label the result "ST increment." If you
prefer the log method of calculation, find the log of
the ST increment in a log table; record and label the
log of the ST increment.
4. Calculate and record the time difference between
the earlier ST and the later ST. Label the result "ST
interval." If calculations are to be completed by the log
method, find the log of the ST interval in a log table,
record and label.
5. Complete this step with either the regular
method of calculation or the log method.
Regular method: Divide the ST increment by the ST
interval to determine the constant ST factor. Record
and label the ST factor. It will be used to correct each
house cusp for time.
Log method: Subtract the log of the ST interval from
the log of the ST increment to determine the log of the
ST factor. Record and label the result; it is a constant
that is used to correct each house cusp for time.
Follow Steps 6-8 to correct the MC. Proceed with
Steps 9-19 to correct all other house cusps for time
and latitude.
6. Record the zodiacal position of the MC that
is listed for the earlier ST.
7. Calculate the cusp increment (correction) for
the MC by either the regular or log method.
Regular method: Multiply the ST factor calculated in
Step 5 by 1 ° (or 60') to determine the cusp increment.
Log method Add the log of the ST factor calculated
in Step 5 to the log of 1Find the anti-log of the result
in a log table. This anti-log is the cusp increment.
8. Add the cusp increment calculated in Step 7
to the earlier position of the MC recorded in Step 6.
The result is the correct MC for the horoscope.
9. Record the position of the house cusp of
interest (not the MC) at the earlier ST and at the later
ST listed for the degree of latitude of the birthplace.
For the present, disregard minutes of latitude.
10. Calculate the difference between the position
of the house cusp of interest at the earlier ST and its
position at the later ST. This difference is the cusp
interval; record and label the cusp interval. Note
whether the house cusp increases (moves forward in
the zodiac) or decreases (moves backward in the zodiac)
as the sidereal time increases. If the log method is being
followed, find the log of the cusp interval and record it.
11. Determine the cusp increment (correction) for
the house cusp of interest by either the regular or log
method.
Regular method: Multiply the cusp interval calculated
in Step 10 by the ST factor calculated in Step 5. The
result is the cusp increment.
Log method: Add the log of the cusp interval
(determined in Step 10) to the log of the ST factor
(found in Step 5). The anti-log of the result is the cusp
increment.
12. Add the cusp increment to the position of the
house cusp of interest, which is listed at the earlier ST
if the cusp increases as the sidereal time increases:
subtract the cusp increment from the earlier position
if the cusp decreases as time increases. It the birthplace
is located at the exact degree of latitude listed in the

=== Page 128 ===
144 Compendium of Astrology
Table of Houses, the result is the correct position of
the house cusp and may be entered in the horoscope.
If the birth latitude contains minutes, this cusp must
be adjusted to the exact latitude of the birthplace
according to the procedure given in Steps 13-19.
13. Record the position of the house cusp of interest
listed at the earlier ST and at the later ST for the latitude
that is 1° greater than the degree of birth latitude
(disregard minutes of birth latitude). Omit this proce-
dure if the cusp distance can be taken directly from the
Table of Houses; instead, record the appropriate cusp
distance (the cusp distance is the difference between the
time corrected position of a cusp at the birth latitude and
its time corrected position at 1° higher latitude). If the
log method is used, record the log of the cusp distance.
Continue with Step 16, omitting Steps 14 and 15.
14. Substituting the cusp positions recorded in
Step 13 for the positions listed at the degree of birth
latitude, follow Steps 10 through 12 to determine the
time corrected cusp at the higher latitude.
15. Calculate the difference between the position
of the time corrected cusp at the degree of birth latitude
and the position of the time corrected cusp at the
higher latitude. The result is the cusp distance; record
it. If the log method of calculation is being used, record
the log of the cusp distance. Note whether the cusp
position increases or decreases as the latitude increases.
16. Record the number of minutes in the birth
latitude that are in excess of an even degree. These extra
minutes are the latitude increment. The latitude interval
is 1° (60'). If logs are used, record the log of the latitude
increment and the log of 1° (latitude interval).
17. Complete this Step by either the regular or log
method of calculation.
Regular method: Divide the latitude increment (from
Step 16) by 60'; the result is the constant latitude
factor. Record and label the constant latitude factor;
it will be used to calculate the latitude correction for
each house cusp except the MC, which needs no
latitude correction.
Log method: Subtract the log of 1° from the log of
the latitude increment calculated in Step 16. Record
the result; it is the log of the latitude factor, a constant
that will be used to correct each house cusp (except
the MC) for latitude.
V
18. Determine the latitude correction with either
the regular method or the tog method.
Regular method: Multiply the cusp distance as
determined in Step 13 or Step 15 by the constant
latitude factor calculated in Step 17. The result is the
correction for latitude.
Log method: Add the log of the cusp distance (from
Step 13 or Step 15) to the log of the latitude factor
determined in Step 17. Find the anti-log of the result
in the log table to determine the latitude correction.
19. Add the correction for latitude, which was
calculated in Step 18, to the position of the time
corrected cusp for the degree of birth latitude (Step
12) if the cusp position increases as latitude increases;
subtract the correction if the position decreases as
latitude increases. Do not apply the latitude correction
to the time corrected cusp for the higher latitude (Step
14). The higher latitude cusp is calculated in order to
determine the correct cusp distance in those instances
when the cusp distance over a given latitude interval
varies at the earlier and later sidereal times of interest.
The correction for latitude is applied to the time
corrected cusp for the degree of birth latitude.
Step 19 completes the calculations necessary to
determine the correct house cusps for a horoscope.
Steps 9-19 are repeated for the Ascendant and the
intermediate house cusps. Tables of Houses list only
six house cusps (1, 2, 3, 10, 11 and 12). An unlisted
house cusp occupies the same degree and opposite sign
that appears on the house cusp that lies directly
opposite it in the horoscope.
Charting Placidean Houses
The houses form the skeleton of the horoscope. After
the house cusps are calculated, they are entered on a
chart form. There are two methods of charting
Placidean houses. In one method the Ascendant is
entered in the eastern section of the horoscope and
labeled according to its zodiacal position. The
remaining house cusps are drawn in at the exact degree
they occupy in the zodiac relative to the Ascendant.
Ecliptic chart forms, which denote degree increments
on the outer circle, are available; the face of the
horoscope is blank. Each cusp line is properly labeled
and drawn from the correct zodiacal degree on the

=== Page 129 ===
Calculation of House Cusps 145
outer circle to the center of the horoscope. Intercepted
signs that do not appear on any house cusp are
enclosed in parentheses or brackets outside the outer
circle at the corresponding zodiacal position. This
method gives a visual representation of the actual sizes
of the houses. Refer to Chapter II, Figure 14.
The more common practice is to correctly label the
zodiacal positions of the house cusps, which appear
on a prepared chart form that is printed with twelve
houses drawn in the face of the horoscope. This so-
called houses chart form is not a replica of the ecliptic:
it represents the houses of the horoscope. These chart
forms depict houses of equal size and look like Equal
House horoscopes. Therefore, one must visualize the
variance in house sizes. An intercepted sign is enclosed
in parentheses or brackets outside the house in which
it is contained. Susan's Tlacidean horoscope is shown
in Chapter 13, Figure 18 and is erected on a houses
chart form. Compare the houses in Susan's horoscope
with the Placidean houses in Chapter 11, Figure 14,
which are drawn on an ecliptic chart form.
Houses based on other quadrant systems (Koch.
Campanus, Regiomontanus, etc.) and Porphyry houses
are charted in the same manner as Placidean houses.
Cusps are corrected by the same procedure using data
from a Table of Houses designed for the particular
method used.
The Equal House Horoscope
For an Equal House horoscope, the MC and Ascendant
are corrected as for a Placidean horoscope; no other
house cusps corrections are necessary. The first house
cusp on a houses chart form (at the eastern point) is
labeled with the zodiacal position of the Ascendant:
all other house cusps (including the tenth) bear the
same degree as the Ascendant. Signs on house cusps
follow in natural order from the Ascendant. The MC,
an angle of the horoscope but not necessarily a house
cusp in this system, is marked at its correct zodiacal
position as is its opposite point, the IC (see Chapter
11, Figure 15).
Charting Houses for an
Unknoion Bhihtune
There are methods, based on actual events in a person's
life, by which an unknown birthtimecan be ascertained
(rectified). A solar chart, which places the first house
cusp in the position of the Sun (conjunct the Sun) as
listed in the ephemeris on the birthdate, is often used
for persons whose birthtimes are uncertain and
unrectified. The houses, called solar houses, follow as
in an Equal Househoroscopewithcuspsignsappearing
in natural sequence beginning with the Sun sign on the
first house. Planetary positions are entered as given in
the ephemeris (uncorrected). A solar chart is not
equivalent to a horoscope erected for the time and
location of birth. It has no Ascendant orMCandany
reference to the Ascendant, MC or other angles is
excluded. Otherwise, houses have the same meaning
as those in a regular horoscope. Interpretation relates
the individuaFs potentials to the Sun, which represents
the self and the life force. Such a chart with its narrow
perspectivegives a somewhat limited view based on the
Sun s influence in the person's life.
Some astrologers prefer to use a sunrise chart, cast
for the time of sunrise on the day of birth at the
birthplace, if the birthtime is uncertain. This type of
chart can be drawn up either as an equal house or
quadrant (Placidean, etc.) horoscope substituting the
time of sunrise for birthtime in calculations. It depicts
the astrological tone set at the beginning of the day,
which has universal application and is, therefore,
applicable to the individual in a general way.
Another method for charting houses when the
birthtime is unknown uses a natural (flat) chart which
has 0° Aries on the cusp of the first house followed
by natural houses and signs as shown in Chapter 1.
Figure 2. This chart shows the relationship between
planets as they appear on the birthdate (as listed in
an ephemeris) and theirnatural signs and houses. Since
each sign and planet has influence in its natural house
in any horoscope, many astrologers believe that the
flat chart more closely describes the individual s needs
motivations and potentials than either a solar or
sunrise chart does.

=== Page 130 ===
146 Compendium of Astrology
Solar, sunrise and flat charts are not utilized
exclusively in connection with unknown birthtimes.
Many astrologers routinely compare these charts with
an individual's horoscope as a means of gaining a more
complete astrological picture.
Locating the Vertex, Anti-Vertex
and East Point
To locate the Vertex (V), find in the Table of Houses
the Ascendant listed for co-latitude (90° minus birth
latitude) under the Midheaven, which equals the natal
IC. The Anti-Vertex (A-V) is the opposite point. For
example, the IC (cusp of the fourth house) for the
horoscope shown in Chapter 11, Figure 14, erected for
41° north latitude, is 1° Leo. The co-latitude for this
chart is 49° (90° — 41°), The Ascendant listed at 49°
under the MC 1° Leo is 24o05' Libra, the Vertex; the
Anti-Vertex is 24° 05' Aries.
The co-latitude of Susan's birthplace is 48° 36' (refer
to Example 2 for birth data); her IC is 1047' Leo.
Interpolation shows that the Vertex for her chart is
at 24047' Libra in the sixth house of her horoscope.
The East Point (E or E. Pt.) is the Ascendant listed
at 0° latitude for the Local Sidereal Time calculated
for a birth, the ST used to find house cusp listings.
If the Table of Houses does not include 0° latitude,
the latitude at the equator, the position of the East
Point can be calculated by adding 6 hours to the Local
Sidereal Time of Birth and finding the MC for this
advanced ST. The East Point at birth is at the same
position as the MC listed for the advanced ST. The
East Point is corrected in the same manner as the MC
if the exact time of interest is not listed. For Susan's
horoscope, the LST is 20:16:07 (Example 2); the
advanced ST is 2:16:07 (20:16:07 + 6:00:00 =
26:16:07, reduced by 24 hours = 2:16:07). The MC
given for the nearest earlier sidereal time is 6° Taurus;
interpolation locates the exact East Point at 6° 21'
Taurus, the same position as listed for 20:16:07, the
LST, at 0° latitude.
The Vertex and East Point may be entered in the
horoscope or listed on the chart form.

Charting the Planets and Moon's Nodes
The planetary positions entered in the ephemeris for a
particular date are exact at the ephemeris reference time
on that date. The listed positions must be adjusted to
account for planetary motion during the time interval
between the GMT birthtime and the GMT ephemeris
reference time. The reference time for a noon ephemeris
is 12:00 p.m. GMT: the reference time for a zero hour
ephemeris is 00:00:00 GMT (12:00 a.m.).
Procedure to Correct the
Zodiacal Longitude of the
Planets and Moon's Nodes
The procedure to determine the exact position of a
planet or node at the time of birth is as follows:
1. Calculate the GMT birthtime. Refer to
Chapter 12, Examples 4, 5 and 6, for this calculation.
Note the GMT birthdate (the date on which the GMT
birthtime falls).
2. Calculate the GMT interval (the time interval
between the GMT birthtime and the GMT reference
time). If a noon ephemeris is used, follow the method
given in Chapter 12. Examples 4 and 5, Step 2, to find
the GMT interval. If a zero hour ephemeris is used,
follow the procedure given in Chapter 12, Example
6, Step 2, to determine the GMT interval. If you use
the regular method of calculation, proceed with Step
3. If you use the log method, record the log of the
GMT interval and continue with Step 4. This log is
the log constant that will be used to calculate the
correction for each planet (node).
3. Calculate the GMT constant (regular method
only; omit this step if you use the log method). If the
GMT interval is an even number of hours (no
minutes), divide the GMT interval by 24 (number of
hours in a day) to determine the GMT constant; if the
GMT interval contains minutes of time, convert the
entire interval to minutes and divide the result by 1440
(number of minutes in a day) to determine the GMT
constant. Record this constant; it will be used to
calculate the correction for each planet (node).
4. Calculate the daily motion for the planet (or
node) of interest. If a noon ephemeris is used, calculate
the difference between the planet's (node's) positions
listed on the GMT birthdate and the preceding date
if the GMT birthtime is a.m.; find the difference
between the planet's (node's) positions listed on the
GMT birthdate and the following date if the GMT
birthtime is p.m. If a zero hour ephemeris is used,
calculate the difference between the planet's (node's)
positions listed on the birthdate and the following date
for both a.m. and p.m. birthtimes. The result is the
daily motion for that planet (node) on the birthdate.
Note whether the planet's motion is direct or
retrograde. The Moon's Node's average motion is
retrograde. Some ephemerides list the position of the
True Node, whose position may differ from that of
the Mean Node, which most ephemerides list, and
whose motion may be direct or retrograde. Use the
True Node's position and motion if it is listed.
5. Calculate the correction in longitude to be
applied to the zodiacal position listed for the planet

=== Page 132 ===
148 Compendium of Astrology
(node) of interest on the GMT birthdate. Use either
the regular method or the log method of calculation.
Regular method: Multiply the daily motion by the GMT
constant. The result is the required correction.
Log method: Add the log of the daily motion to the
log constant. The anti-log of this result is the required
correction.
6. Correct the planet's (node's) position that is
listed on the GMT birthdate. To correct the position
of a planet that is in direct motion, proceed as follows:
If a noon ephemeris is used, subtract the correction
derived in Step 5 from the planet's position listed on
the GMT birthdate if the GMTbirthtime is a.m.; add
the correction to the listed position if the GMT
birthtime is p.m. If a zero hour ephemeris is used, add
the correction to the position listed on the GMT
birthdate. To correct the position of a planet in
retrograde motion, add the correction for an a.m. birth
when using a noon ephemeris; subtract the correction
for a p.m. birth when using a noon ephemeris; subtract
the correction for all births when using a zero hour
ephemeris. The result gives the correct zodiacal
position of the planet (node) at the time of birth.

Entering the Planets and Nodes
in the Chart Form
Before the planets are entered in the horoscope, it is
good practice to check the approximate position of the
Sun in the horoscope against the birthtime. Think of
the horoscope as a clock with each house representing
a two-hour interval. Place 6:00 a.m. at the Ascendant,
12:00 noon at the MC, 6:00 p.m. at the Descendant and
12:00 midnight at the IC. The Sun should occupy the
section of the horoscope that represents the actual

=== Page 135 ===
Charting the Planets ami Moon 's Nodes 151
birth time (not the GMT birthtime or the Local Sidereal
Time ot birth). If the Sun is not at the approximate
position that corresponds to the actual birthtime,
recheck the calculations for the Local Sidereal Time and
the house cusps. The house cusps are probably
positioned incorrectly. Bear in mind that the Sun's
position in the horoscope may not correlate exactly with
this astrological clock. The Ascendant is more correctly
associated with sunrise, which may occur earlier or later
than 6:00 a.m. However, if the Sun does not fall within
a few degrees of the house that corresponds to the
birthtime, calculations should be checked.
The planets and the Moon's North Node are entered
in the horoscope according to their corrected positions.
The Moon's South Node may be omitted, but it is
understood that the South Node occupies the point
in the zodiac and the horoscope that lies directly
opposite the position of the North Node.
The planets and the signs they occupy are designated
in the horoscope by the corresponding glyphs.
Planetary glyphs (symbols) are entered in the face of
the horoscope near the outer ring. The zodiacal
position may be written from left to right or vertically,
whichever is more legible. The notation for the
zodiacal position may precede or follow the planetary
glyph. All planetary entries (glyphs and position
designations) are placed within the outer circle and
written so they may be read from a normal reading
position without turning the horoscope around. Styles
vary, but it is common practice to insert the sign
designation between the degrees and minutes of
zodiacal longitude, as is displayed in Figure 18.
The placement of the planets in the horoscope depends
upon the house system and type of chart form used. For
a Placidean horoscope charted on an ecliptic chart form,
a small tick is placed on the outer circle at the zodiacal
degree a planet occupies; the correct planetary entry is
written opposite the tick inside the circle.
For a Placidean horoscope charted on a houseschart
form, the planets are placed in correct zodiacal sequence
close to the house cusp that bears the same sign as the
planet. If two house cusps bear the same sign as a planet,
the planet is placed near the cusp to which the planet
lies closest in the zodiac. Correct zodiacal sequence is
always observed; a planet is placed on the side of the
house cusp according to where it falls in the natural
order of the zodiac. A planet in an intercepted sign is
placed near the center of the house it occupies. Parallel
lines that intersect the outer circle may be drawn on each
side of a planet to indicate interception, but this is not
necessary if the intercepted sign is correctly indicated
by brackets outside the circle. Figure 18 shows Susan's
Placidean horoscope charted on a houses chart form.

Declinations
The declinations listed in the ephemeris are corrected
in a manner similar to that used to correct the zodiacal
positions of the planets. The procedure is the same;
the daily travel of declination replaces daily motion
in the calculations. To determine the correction for
declination, the daily travel of declination is multiplied
by the GMT constant (the same GMT constant used
to correct the planets' zodiacal longitude), or, if the
log method is preferred, the log of travel is added to
the log constant (the same log constant used to correct
planetary positions). If the ephemeris used does not
list declinations for each day. daily travel is based on
the average travel per day during the time span
between entries. Declinations for an unlisted date are
interpolated according to the two consecutive entries
between which the date of interest falls.

=== Page 136 ===
152 Compendium of Astrology
When calculating the daily travel of declination,
record the direction of declination, N (north of the
celestial equator) or S (south of the celestial equator).
Note whether the declination is increasing numerically
or decreasing. The correction for increasing declination
is added to or subtracted from the listed declination
according to the rules for correcting a planet in direct
motion; decreasing declination is treated in the same
manner as a retrograde planet. If a planet crosses the
celestial equator (0° declination) from N to S or vice
versa, the declination will decrease to 0° and then
increase. The correction is treated accordingly.

Most chart forms provide a space in which to enter
the corrected declinations. If no space is provided, the
declinations are listed on the chart form wherever there
is room. The declinations may be written with the N
or S following the degrees and minutes.
The declinations for the Ascendant and MC are listed
on the chart form with the planetary declinations. The
declination of the Ascendant is the same as that of the
Sun at the time the Sun occupies the same zodiacal
position as the Ascendant: the declination of the MC is
the same as that of the Sun at the time the Sun occupies
the position of the MC. In order to determine the
declination of the Ascendant, find the date in the
ephemeris on which the Sun is in the same zodiacal
position as the Ascendant; the declination of the Sun
listed on that date is the declination of the Ascendant.
If the exact position of interest is not listed, the
declination entered on the date on which the Sun's
position is closest to the Ascendant's position can be
corrected by interpolation. The declination for the MC
is found in the same way.
Some ephemerides do not list the declination of the
Moon's North Node. If the Node's declination is not
listed, follow the same procedure used to determine
the declinations for the Ascendant and MC to estimate
the declination for the Node.
The Part of Fortune
The Part of Fortune (Pars Fortunae) is a
sensitive point in the horoscope that lies a
distance from the Ascendant equal to the
distance the Moon lies from the Sun. The
symbol for the Part of Fortune is similar to
that for Earth; an X is placed inside the circle instead
of the cross, which symbolizes Earth.
The Part of Fortune, most widely used of the
numerous Arabic Parts, is considered a fortunate point
that shows by house position the area in which one's
endeavors are most apt to reap success and by sign
position one's approach to these endeavors. Refer to
Appendix C for information about other Arabic Parts.
Success indicated by the Part of Fortune does not
necessarily denote material gains. Intellectual accom-
plishments, good health, or the vicarious success one
experiences through achievements of his or her children
are among the possible benefits associated with the Part
of Fortune depending upon sign and house placement;
it is read in context with the overall horoscope.
An adversely aspected Part of Fortune, especially
if it is in the sign of Pisces, may be termed the "Part
of Misfortune," for little benefit is likely to manifest.
To calculate the Part of Fortune, the position of the
Moon is added to the position of the Ascendant; the
position of the Sun is subtracted from this sum. The
signs are designated by number according to their
natural position in the zodiac (Aries = 1, Taurus =
2, Gemini = 3, etc.). The full circle of 12 signs may
be added if necessary to carry out the subtraction. One
sign may be converted to 30 degrees in order to
complete calculations. The final result is reduced to
lowest units. There can be no more than 12 signs, 29
degrees, or 59 minutes in the final answer (60' = 1°;
30° = 1 sign). The sign number is replaced by the
usual sign designation.

Aspects Defined
Aspects depend upon the angular distance between
two planets or the distance between a planet and an
important point in the horoscope such as an angle or
house cusp, the Moon's Nodes or the Part of Fortune.
Aspects provide the means of planetary interaction.
Planets in aspect influence each other's action according
to the type of aspect and the nature of the planets forming
the aspect. The relationships that planets bear to each
other through aspects in the natal horoscope constitute
patterns of experience and development that are unique
to the individual. Aspects give the astrologer a more
complete picture of planetary influence in the horoscope.
Calculation and Tabulation of Aspects
All aspects except the parallel and the contraparallel
are defined by a specified number of degrees, which
separate two points in the zodiac. Parallels and
contraparallels are defined by declination. Two planets
that occupy the same numerical degree and direction
of declination (both planets either north or south) are
said to be parallel. Two planets which occupy the same
numerical degree of declination with one planet north
and the other south are contraparallel.
The point at which an aspect is exact to the degree
and minute is termed partile. An aspect that is within
1° of partile, is called an exact aspect; however, an
aspect need not be exact to be effective. The number
of degrees by which an aspect may vary from partile
is called the orb of influence. An aspect that is not
exact but still falls within the allowable orb is termed
a platic aspect. The closer an aspect is to partile (the
smaller the orb), the stronger its influence.
Aspects fall into two general categories, major and
minor. Major aspects are more powerful and
influential in the horoscope than are minor aspects.

The orb for all minor aspects is 2°. The semi-sextile,
semi-square, sesquiquadrate and quincunx are usually
the only minor aspects studied in a natal horoscope.
Some astrologers consider the quincunx a major aspect
and weight it accordingly. The influence of the other
minor aspects is slight. Nevertheless, these aspects form
links between planetary energies, however weak.
Frequently, the less important aspects support stronger
indications in the horoscope.
The faster moving planet of two in aspect is called
the significator, the slower moving planet is the
promittor. The significator is said to aspect the
promittor; the promittor is said to be in aspect with
the significator. With the exception of solar aspects,
the order in which natal aspects are written is
significator, aspect, promittor. It is customary to list
the Sun first regardless of whether it is the significator
or promittor. For example, a conjunction between the
luminaries is usually written Sun conjunct Moon
(O cf I)) although the Moon as the fastest moving of
all the planets is the significator in any aspect it forms.
When a planet is retrograde, stationary or approaching
transition from direct to retrograde or vice versa, its
motion may be slower than average. Check the daily
motion on the birthdate to determine the correct
significator if in doubt.
If the significator is moving toward but has not
reached the point of partile, the aspect is said to be
applying (forming); if the significator is past and
moving away from the point of partile, the aspect is
separating (receding). An applying aspect indicates a
condition, experience, action, state of mind or
development that will become evident as the life of
the individual progresses. A separating aspect suggests
that which is a part of the individual's experience or
character at birth: one's unaquired characteristics,
innate knowledge or instincts, one's heredity, one's
prenatal experience, perhaps one's karma.
In order to calculate aspects, one usually starts with
the Sun and counts the number of degrees that separate
the Sun and other occupied points in the horoscope.
Aspects may be counted forward or backward in the
zodiac. If the direction from significator to promittor
is forward in the zodiac (counterclockwise in the
horoscope), the aspect is called approaching because
the significator is approaching the point occupied by
the planet it aspects. If the direction from significator
to promittor is backward in the zodiac (clockwise in
the horoscope), the aspect is termed departing because
the significator is departing from (leaving) the point
occupied by the promittor.
Do not confuse the terms applying and separating with
the terms approaching and departing. Applying and
separating aspects depend upon the partile point of the
aspect; approaching and departing aspects are based on
the zodiacal direction from the significator to the
promittor. An approaching aspect may be either
applying or separating, as can a departing aspect.
An approaching aspect is given a broader, more
outward and social significance than a departing aspect;
it is considered more overt in manifestation. A departing
aspect has a more personal and subjective influence; it
is given a subtle and somewhat fatalistic connotation.
The Moon's aspects are calculated after the Sun's. One
proceeds to do the same with each remaining planet in
order of swiftest moving to slowest.
The conjunction and opposition are fairly easy to
recognize. Planets that lie side by side in the horoscope
are conjunct if within orb; planets opposite each other
in the horoscope are in opposition if within orb. For
example, a planet in 5°21' Sagittarius is conjunct any
planet that is posited between 27°21' Scorpio and 13° 21'
Sagittarius; it is in opposition with any planet that falls
between 27°21' Taurus and 13<,21' Gemini. The orb is
8° on either side of partile, which gives a 16° span of
influence. A conjunction that is formed between planets
in different signs is a dissociate conjunction; an
opposition that occurs between planets in signs not
directly opposite each other in thezodiac is a dissociate
opposition. If a planet is within orb but occupies a sign
different from that of the partile point, the asepct formed
is called dissociate.
Planets that are within a 6° orb and 60° apart form
a sextile. If a planet occupies the beginning or ending
degrees of a sign, it may form sextiles with planets that
are one, two or three signs away. A planet in lo30'
Taurus can form a sextile with any planet posited
between 25°30' Aquarius (three signs from Taurus)
and 7°30' Pisces (two signs from Taurus), and it can
form a sextile with any planet that falls between
25<,30' Gemini (one sign from Taurus) and 7°30'
Cancer (two signs from Taurus). A sextile formed from
Taurus to Aquarius or Pisces is a departing sextile
(backward in the natural order of the zodiac); a sextile
from Taurus to Gemini or Cancer is an approaching
sextile (forward in the zodiac). A sextile formed

=== Page 141 ===
Aspects Defined 157 *
between a planet in Taurus and one in Aquarius or
Gemini is a dissociate sextile.
Planets that occupy different signs of the same
quadruplicity and are not opposite each other form
a square aspect if within orb. In Susan's horoscope
(Chapter 13, Figure 18) Mars in 17° 59' Capricorn (a
cardinal sign) squares Neptune in 18° 48' Libra (a
cardinal sign). Mars is the significator (it moves faster
than Neptune). The square is exact (the orb is 49', the
difference between Mars' position and partile). It is
applying (Mars is moving toward partile, which is
18°48' Capricorn) and departing (the direction of the
aspect from the significator, Mars, to Neptune is
clockwise in the horoscope: Mars is moving away
from Neptune's position).
A dissociate square is formed between planets within
orb that are posited in signs belonging to different
quadruplicities. The Sun in Susan's horoscope, placed
at 7°05' Sagittarius (a mutable sign), squares Jupiter
in 29°46' Aquarius (a fixed sign). The aspect isplatic;
the orb is a wide 7° 19'. The aspect is separating and
approaching; the Sun is moving away from the point
of partile (29° 46' Scorpio); the direction of the square
from the Sun (significator) to Jupiter (promittor) is
forward in the zodiac and counterclockwise in the
horoscope.
Planets that occupy different signs of the same
triplicity are in trine if the degrees are in orb. In Susan's
horoscope the Moon at 4° 38' Leo (a fire sign) trinesboth
the Sun at 7°05' Sagittarius and Venus at 11°00'
Sagittarius (a fire sign). Both trines are platic, applying
and approaching. A trine is dissociate if it is fonned
between planets that belong to different triplicities.
Parallels and contraparallels are easy to identify
from the declinations listed on the chart form; they
can be separated by no more than 1°.
Of the important minor aspects, the semi-sextile and
the quincunx are theeasiest to calculate. The semi-sextile
is formed by planets that are within 2° (orb) of being
30° (one full sign) apart; the quincunx is formed by
planets that lie within 2° orb and are five signs apart.
The semi-square and the sesquiquadrate are more
difficult to recognize. It may be helpful to add 15° to the
actual degrees a planet occupies and then count forward
one sign or backward two signs for the semi-square and
count forward four signs or backward five signs for the
sesquiquadrate. For example, a planet in 5° Leo forms
a semi-square with one in 20° (5° + 15°) Virgo or
Gemini; the same planet can form a sesquiquadrate with
a planet in 20° Sagittarius or Pisces. If this method is
confusing, the actual degrees must be counted until one
becomes familiar with these aspects.
Most chart forms display an aspectarian similar to
the one shown in Figure 19. As the aspects are
calculated they are entered by symbol in the
aspectarian. Zodiacal aspects are placed in the right
diagonal half of the aspectarian; parallels and
contraparallels are listed in the left diagonal. Aspects
to the Ascendant and MC are entered in the two
bottom rows of the aspectarian in the column headed
by the aspecting planet. Planets that aspect the
Descendant or IC form complementary aspects with
the Ascendant or MC respectively; these aspects are
listed according to the aspect formed with the
Ascendant or MC. All aspects to the North Node and
Part of Fortune, including parallels and contra-
parallels, are entered in the corresponding column in
the row headed by the aspecting planet. Aspects to
the South Node (complementary aspects of the North
Node) are not recorded in the aspectarian.
