Aspects of the Moon's Nodes and Part of Fortune
Aspects formed between the Moon's Nodes and Part
of Fortune, and aspects that the Nodes and Part of
Fortune form with the Ascendant and MC are
unimportant unless a planet aspects the Nodes or Part
of Fortune. Planets energize the horoscope; the Nodes
and Part of Fortune do not.
Conjunctions and oppositions that occur between
these points are more significant than other mutual
aspects. An opposition is automatically formed by the
opposite Node or angle if a Node or angle forms a
mutual conjunction or conjuncts the Part of Fortune.
If a planet aspects the conjunction, energy is focused
in the house in which the conjunction occurs.
Other major aspects that occur between the Nodes,
Part of Fortune and angles link the interests of the houses
involved. Interpretation depends upon the natures of
planets that aspect these points and the type of planetary
aspects formed. Minor aspects are meaningless.
Mutual aspects between the Ascendant and MC are
not interpreted as such. The orientation between the
angles as it varies from the norm (square) distorts the
size of the houses and quadrants, placing emphasis on
the larger portions.

Astrological Guidance in Planning for the Future
Various techniques are available by which one can
obtain greater insight into the potentials indicated in
the natal chart and developments that take place
during a lifetime. They help the individual achieve
greater self-understanding, improve relationships and
know the time of life when certain courses of action
are most apt to be beneficial. More importantly,
through these studies one becomes increasingly aware
that the direction a natal potential takes is in his or
her hands. When personal decisions and actions are
based on the proper utilization of astrological
influences, a person gains greater control over the
cause and effect of life.
Progressions and Transits
A progressed horoscope updates a natal horoscope: it
reveals developmental patterns and emerging trends as
they unfold according to the promise of the natal chart.
A natal horoscope never loses its initial character, but
it is no more static than life itself, for it describes an on-
going growth process. For example, when a person's
natal Sun progresses into the next sign, that person does
not lose original Sun-sign characteristics; he or she gains
added perspective through new Sun-sign qualities. One
can most successfully fulfill certain potentials and realize
particular goals when the flow ol creative energies shown
by the progressed horoscope harmonizes with and
centers on associated areas. For instance, when planets
progress to the tenth house or aspect the MC or its
planetary ruler, career development is emphasized.
The most common method of progressing a
horoscope, the "day for a year" method, relates each
successive day after birth to one year of life. Beginning
with the GMT birthdate and counting it zero, the
number of days that corresponds to one's age in years
is counted forward in the ephemeris to obtain the
progressed ephemeris date (FED). The progressed
horoscope is calculated in the same manner as the natal
chart (Chapters 12 and 13) using the time and location
of birth but substituting astrological data (sidereal
time, planetary positions, etc.) listed in the ephemeris
on the FED for that given on the birthdate.
For example, to progress Susan's horoscope to age
eighteen, one would use the data given in the
ephemeris for December 17, 1950, eighteen days after
her GMT birthdate, November 29, 1950. Refer to
Chapter 12, Example 2, for Susan's birth data. House
cusps and planetary positions are corrected as for the
natal chart. The horoscope erected for this date, the
FED for Susan's eighteenth year, is exact on her
eighteenth birthday, November 29, 1963.
The progressed horoscope may be drawn up on a
separate chart form, but it is easier to see how the
progressed chart relates to the natal horoscope by
marking progressed positions outside the natal wheel.
Special chart forms that contain an outer wheel designed
for progressed planets are available. When using this
type of form, it is customary to insert the progressed
planets. Ascendant and MC, but not other house cusps.
The "solar-arc" method is used by some to advance
the house cusps for a progressed horoscope. With this
procedure, the Sun's travel between the birthdate and
the FED is calculated; the result (in degrees and
minutes) is added to the natal MC to determine the
progressed MC. The Ascendant and other house cusps
listed in the Table of Houses at the birth latitude that

=== Page 222 ===
248 Compendium of Astrology
correspond to the progressed MC become the
progressed house cusps.
Instead of correcting progressed planets to the GMT
birthtime, positions listed on the PED may be entered
in the progressed horoscope. These positions are exact
on the Adjusted Calculation Date (ACD), a date
different from the birthday. To find the ACD, add the
GMT interval (Chapter 12) as calculated for the natal
horoscope to the sidereal time listed in a noon
ephemeris on the GMT birthdate if the GMT birthtime
is a.m. (opposite procedure than when calculating the
local sidereal time of birth); leaf forward in the
ephemeris to find this sidereal time; the corresponding
date is the ACD. For an afternoon birth (GMT),
subtract the GMT interval from the ST listed on the
birthdate (noon ephermis); leaf back in the ephemeris
to find the date which corresponds to the calculated
ST. If a zero hour ephemeris is used, the GMT interval
is always subtracted from the ST listed on the
birthdate, and the ACD always occurs on a date prior
to birth. The ACD and birthdate coincide only if the
GMT birthtime is the same as the ephemeris reference
time (noon or midnight). The ACD is a constant date
that applies to any given year.
To calculate the ACD for Susan's chart, the GMT
interval, 9:05 (GMT birthtime is 9:05 p.m. ), is subtracted
from 16:30:13, the ST listed in a noon ephemeris on her
birthdate. (Refer to Chapter 11, Figure 16.) The result,
7:26:13, is unlisted. The date on which the closest ST,
7:27:08, is entered and on which the calculated ST does
occur, July 14, is selected as her ACD.
The ACD is a constant that applies to any given
year. The planetary positions listed on December 17,
1950 (PED for Susan's eighteenth year), uncorrected,
are the progressed positions exact on July 14, 1968,
the ACD for the eighteenth year after birth. If the
positions listed on the PED are corrected to the GMT
birth interval, they are exact on the birthday of the
year that corresponds to the PED.
Planetary positions are corrected or, alternatively,
the ACD used so that one can determine by
interpolation the date on which a progressed aspect
is exact, the time when its influence is strongest. The
orb for a progressed aspect is 1°. The progressed Moon
moves about Is each month, so its position is
interpolated for each month. Its aspects are influential
for about two months, one month applying and one
month separating. A progressed aspect may be in orb
for two or three years, or for a lifetime, depending
upon the rate of planetary travel. Heavier planets
progress so slowly that the only changes likely are
those associated with closing (reaching partile) or
separating from (going beyond orb limits) a natal
aspect. The progressed influence of these planets is
more psychological than physical unless natal or other
progressed indications support physical manifestation.
If an outer planet occupies the first or last degrees of
a sign, it may progress into the next sign or retrograde
into the previous one. House changes are also possible
for these planets if they are placed natally near a cusp.
Such changes alter planetary expression and activity
according to progressed sign and house positions.
A progressed horoscope is read in conjunction with
the natal horoscope. Progressed indications that are
not confirmed natally are meaningless and inapplicable
to that individual. In order that an aspect between two
progressed planets or a progressed and natal planet
relate to the individual, the two planets must relate
to each other in the natal chart, although they do not
have to be in aspect natally. For example, Susan's
progressed horoscope for 1968 showed that Mars had
progressed into Aquarius and into the natal tenth
house, forming a trine with progressed Satum. These
two planets form no natal aspect, but Satum disposits
Mars natally and therefore influences its action.
Satum, natural ruler of the tenth house, also co-rules
the natal tenth and is co-dispositor (with Uranus) of
progressed Mars. The progressed trine, significant
because it is a major aspect and because Mars and
Satum are related natally and associated with the tenth
house (natal Mars in Capricorn, the natural sign of
the tenth house), indicates conditions favorable to
career interests and other tenth house affairs. It also
influences other interests ruled in the natal horoscope
by Mars and Satum.
Aspects formed between progressed planets and
angles are not as influential as progressed/natal
aspects, but if a natal relationship exists between the
aspected planets, the progressed aspect activates natal
indications. For example, the Mars/Satum trine in
Susan's progressed horoscope, a progressed/progres-
sed aspect, energizes the natal Satum/MC trine that
is present in her natal horoscope (both planets have
tenth house influence). More importantly, it extends
and reinforces the influence of a trine between pro-
gressed Mars and natal Satum that occurred during

=== Page 223 ===
Astrological Guidance in Planning for the Future 249
Susan's sixteenth year and was still effective when the
progressed/progressed trine reached beginning orb
limits. However, at that time. Mars remained in the
ninth house, which Satum rules natally, placing
emphasis on education and linking educational and
career interests. In retrospect, it appears that the time
was ripe for Susan to seriously prepare for her career
or for advanced studies in connection with her
profession.
The Ascendant and MC, key points in a horoscope,
externalize indications shown in a natal horoscope
when aspected by progressed planets. Hard aspects,
especially the conjunction, formed by progressed
planets to natal angles or by progressed angles to natal
planets, describe significant events in the life of an
individual. Aspects involving the Ascendant are
associated with happenings of a personal nature, inner
changes, and events that affect the body, Midheaven
events deal with external conditions and activities.
A progressed horoscope shows the major influences
that operate during a given year. Transits, the
movements of planets on a particular day identified
by planetary positions listed in the ephemeris for
that date, describe astrological influences operating on
the day of interest. Hard aspects to natal or progressed
planets formed by fast-moving transiting planets
frequently trigger or time events indicated in the
horoscope. Transiting aspects (hard) to the angles
also time events as do conjunctions to cusps of houses
that rule affairs activated by progressed aspects. The
transiting Moon, which moves about 10 every two
hours, frequently times events almost to the minute
if the birthtime and horoscope are accurate. If the
horoscope is inexact, timing of events is unpredictable.
The progressed Moon, when it conjuncts a planet,
angle or house cusp of interest, indicates the time
of an event to the day or even closer if calculations
are correct.
Easy progressed aspects describe conditions and
circumstances that affect related affairs; hard
progressed and transiting aspects are associated with
specific events such as marriage, surgery, childbirth
or a career change. The progressed Mars/Saturn trine
(an easy aspect) in Susan's horoscope described
conditions that could be helpful to career advancement
during 1968; it did not signify a specific event.
However, during the same period, progressed Mars
conjuncted her natal MC, an aspect associated with
external events. Transiting Mars conjuncted natal
Satum effective November 9, 10 (exact) and 11 (1° orb)
and conjuncted progressed Satum on November 10,
11, 12 (exact) and 13, indicating the possible
manifestation of a tenth house event associated with
favorable conditions denoted by the trine. The
transiting Moon exactly opposed the natal MC
(conjunct an angle, the IC) and squared progressed
Saturn on November 11 when she was given a
promotion. The potential for the event stemmed from
the progressed Mars/MC conjunction; the progressed
Mars/Saturn trine set the stage with helpful
conditions; the transiting Mars/Saturn conjunctions
triggered the promotion; the transiting Moon/MC
opposition timed the action.
A transiting planet cannot time an event that is
not indicated in the horoscope. Bear in mind that
the transiting Moon completes a circuit of the
horoscope every month and forms every possible
aspect with every planet and angle each month. When
they aspect the natal horoscope, fast moving transits
indicate daily activities such as shopping (Venus),
visiting (Mercury), etc.
Heavy transiting planets give general indications of
current trends shown by the houses and signs they
occupy and the aspects they form with natal or
progressed planets. The duration of their aspects varies
from ten days to several months depending upon their
rates of motion at the time.
The impact of progressed and transiting planets
depends largely upon their significance in the natal
chart. A person reacts more pronouncedly to influ-
ences generated by progressed and transiting planets
that are strong natally and to the chart ruler than to
influences generated by planets weak in the natal chart.
In assessing predominant influences for a given year,
eclipse events that occur during that year are
considered. The affairs of a house in which a transiting
solar eclipse falls are emphasized until the next eclipse
occurs, usually about six months later. If the eclipse
aspects natal planets or angles, its influence is directed
according to aspect and natal indications. A transiting
lunar eclipse supports and clarifies the solar eclipse that
it accompanies.
Each month, the natal house and sign in which the
lunation (new Moon) occurs give clues to the type of
activities and events that can be successfully initiated
or changed unless the new Moon afflicts planets in the

=== Page 224 ===
250 Compendium of Astrology
natal chart; then a steady policy is best, and all but
absolutely necessary changes are inadvisable.
Converse Directions
Converse directions progress a horoscope "backwards."
Procedure to erect a converse chart is the same as the
"day for a year" method of progressing a horoscope
except that one counts backward in time from the
birthdate the number of years of interest to find the
converse ephemeris date (CED) for which the converse
horoscope is cast.
A converse horoscope gives insight into innate
behavior patterns and karma. To more fully understand
the potentials that appear in a horoscope progressed to
a given year after birth, one studies a converse chart
erected for the same number of years before birth.
Astrological factors that link the natal, progressed and
converse charts give clues to karmic problems as
described by natal and converse ties and point out the
means by which karmic relationships can be best worked
out as shown by corresponding progressed indications.
Converse charts reveal hidden aspects of the
personality such as latent talent and deep-seated
psychological motivations. They are helpful in
uncovering the root causes of emotional or psychological
conflicts and in resolving problems.
Solar and Lunar Returns
Solar and lunar returns provide information that
elaborates on that found in the natal and progressed
horoscopes. A solar return, erected according to the
date and time in a given year that the Sun returns to
the zodiacal position it occupies in the natal horoscope
and the location in which the individual resides on that
date, indicates by the Sun's house position the main
emphasis of interest for that year. Influences operative
during that year based on the solar return as a whole
(planets, signs, houses and aspects) corroborate
information found in the progressed horoscope and
give additional details concerning progressed general
trends. For example, a progressed Uranus aspect is in
force for several years; a solar return may contain
supplementary information that clarifies the
progressed Uranian influence and further defines
potential Uranian events.
A lunar return, based on the date and time each
month that the Moon returns to its natal zodiacal
position and the individual's place of residence on that
date, gives a view of developments that occur from
the time of the chart to the time of the Moon's next
return the following month. The Moon's position and
aspects describe activities and interests that influence
the individual on a personal level and often affect the
emotions. By providing a monthly outlook a lunar
return pinpoints more closely events and situations
described in the solar return and progressed horoscope.
Synastry
No one person reacts to any two other people in the
same way. Lack of understanding can undermine
relationships that might otherwise be productive.
Through synastry techniques, valuable insights into
the marital or love relationships, the parent/child
relationship, friendships, business affiliations and
other associations can be gained, insights that enable
people to recognize and understand each other's needs
and to identify those factors upon which the success
of a relationship depends. Comparison and composite
charts are the two most useful tools available to the
astrologer for determining strengths and weaknesses
inherent in relationships.
Comparison Charts
The basis for a relationship, potential problem areas
and strong points can be determined by comparing the
natal potentials of the persons involved, noting
similarities and differences in the charts and aspects
between the planets and angles of one chart and those
of the other. Findings are assessed on the basis of
compatibility and mutual ties (aspects). Differences are
not necessarily incompatible; they may be complemen-
tary. For instance, what one person lacks the other
may contribute to balance relationship needs.
To analyze a relationship involving two people, two
comparison charts, often referred to as compatibility
charts, are erected. To do this, the planets and angles
from one partner's horoscope are inserted into the
natal chart of the other and vice versa. A balance of
elements and modes in the two charts is desirable
although not essential to sustaining the relationship.
Imbalance adds a narrow perspective. For example,
if the combined charts show a predominance of water

=== Page 225 ===
Astrological Guidance in Planning for the Future 251
signs and lack of earth, these people react to each other
emotionally with little concern for practical aspects
of the relationship. If fixed signs predominate and
mutable are lacking, the relationship is rigid. Such
imbalance may not harm the relationship; in fact, it
might be appropriate to the association and to the
individuals involved. Examination of the natal charts
indicates each person's needs as individuals and as
participants in a relationship: comparison charts show
how each responds to the other's needs and what each
contributes to and gains from the relationship.
The house that a partner's planets occupy in one's
natal chart describe the role the partner plays. The
main concept in role playing is indicated by the Sun,
for the position of a partner's Sun in one's natal chart
shows how the individual relates to the partner's
personality. For example, if a woman's Sun occupies
the fourth house in a man's natal chart, he sees her
as someone to look after his needs much as his mother
did when he was a child; if a man's Sun appears in
a woman's fourth house, she relates to him as a father-
figure. The position of the Moon describes the
emotional response, Mercury the intellectual, Venus
the affectional and Mars the sexual. Jupiter indicates
areas in which one partner benefits the other. Saturn
points out areas of restriction, indicating one's
responsibility to the partner within the framework of
the relationship.
Aspects (use one-half natal orb) indicate specific
potentials and qualities of the relationship. Afflictions
indicate potential problems; easy aspects describe
helpful bonds based on common interests or
characteristics according to the natures of the planets
forming the aspects.
A relationship may be fruitful for a limited time
period only. A conjunction to one of the angles in a
natal horoscope by a partner's natal planet yields clues
to the durability of the association; progressed
indications describe its future and probable duration.
If several persons are involved, which is often the
case in business associations, each natal chart is
compared with every other. Utilization of a composite
chart, which incorporates all relationship potentials
into a single horoscope, reduces to one the number
of charts needed to assess a relationship.
Composite Charts
A composite chart is one that describes a relationship
as an entity. It is erected by plotting the midpoints
between like planets and angles of one natal chart with
that of the partner(s). It reveals the combined
potentials of the persons involved in terms of their
association, not in terms of individual needs and
contributions. Some astrologers prefer composite
techniques, others comparison, but most utilize both
methods when applicable to gain a clearer picture of
a relationship and the role each member plays.
To delineate a composite chart, natal interpretations
are adapted to relationship symbolism. Signs and planets
associated with the houses give a general view of
relationship potentials and areas of primary interest;
aspects (natal orbs applicable) point to particulars. For
example, a well-aspected Jupiter in the tenth house of
a composite chart suggests that members of the
association can, working together, accomplish goals of
the relationship; in the second house, it suggests that
financial benefits can accrue as a result of combined
activities. Jupiter afflictions bring out extravagances and
excesses associated with the planet.
The Sun represents the lifeline of a relationship. Well
aspected, it indicates a vital, viable association. Sun
afflictions drain and endanger a relationship, although
accompanying easy solar aspects reinforce Sun
energies and revitalize the association.
Composite charts are especially helpful in assessing
associations that involve large numbers of people such
as corporation boards and organizational committees.
Astrological Techniques Designed
for Specialized Needs
Refined methods, developed to enlighten the individual
in order that he or she can make correct decisions and
act to best advantage on matters of specific interest,
give guidance concerning current everyday affairs as
well as once-in-a-lifetime activities.
Relocation Charts
Contemplating a move? Erect a relocation chart to
determine the area that is most advantageous in
relation to your natal potentials. A relocation chart
is calculated for the time and date of birth and
longitude and latitude of the contemplated site. It the
distance between the new location and the place of
birth is small, only negligible differences may exist
between the relocation and natal charts. It a large
distance is involved, the zodiacal positions of the
planets remain the same as in the natal chart, but house

=== Page 226 ===
252 Compendium of Astrology
cusps and the house positions of planets change in the
relocation chart. It is desirable to choose a location
that produces a horoscope that places planetary
emphasis in the houses of one's main interests. For
example, if natal Jupiter is in the first or third house,
a different location might shift it to the second house,
thus improving moneymaking potentials.
Election Charts
Election charts are erected to find the best time to imple-
ment specific plans. For example, if one is planning to
embark on a business venture, a day within the tentative
time frame (on which transiting planets, especially those
which bear upon the business, are making favorable
aspects) is chosen as the beginning date. The time that
corresponds to the Midheaven or Ascendant, which
most closely relates to the nature of the business and ties
in with relevant houses or planets in the natal chart, is
selected as a possible opening or beginning time, and a
chart is erected for the tentative time, date and site of
the opening. The time and house cusps are adjusted to
place planets of significance where their influence will
be most beneficial, and malefics in houses that are not
directly connected with the business, its finances,
customers, etc. The application of election charts is
almost unlimited; they are helpful in determining when
to get married, travel, seek promotion or apply for a job,
sign important papers, purchase or sell property, invest,
make changes, or to begin activities of any nature.
Horary Charts
Horary charts, closely allied to election charts, are
designed to answer specific questions of interest. They
are constructed according to the date and time the
question is first proposed (mentally or verbally) and
the location of the querent, the person who asks the
question. If the initial time is unknown, the time at
which the client first approaches the astrologer with
the question (by mail, telephone or in person) is used.
Information about lost articles, missing persons,
contemplated actions or decisions (Is it to my
advantage to accept the job offer? Is the partnership
opportunity with Mr. Jones beneficial to me? Is it wise
to invest in U.S. Steel shares at the present time?) is
contained in horary charts. The first house of a horary
chart rules the querent (questioner); the house that is
naturally associated with the matter of interest rules
the query (the matter inquired about). Study of the
planetary rulers of the houses of the querent and the
query and the Moon, which describes by its aspects
the dynamics of the chart (action or lack of it), reveals
the answer to the question; irrelevant elements of the
horary chart are disregarded. For example, if one
wishes to locate a misplaced sum of personal cash, the
sign and house positions and aspects of the planetary
rules of the Ascendant (querent) and the second house
(query, personal money) and the Moon and the
interrelationships that exist among these three planets
describe if, where and when the money can be found.
Astrological factors that have no bearing on the
question are not considered.
Medical Astrology
Medical astrology is a highly specialized field that
requires knowledge of the functioning of the human
body and psyche as well as relationships of planets
and signs to minerals, vitamins, enzymes, bacteria and
other disease-producing agents, all parts of the body
and body systems. It is limited by law to diagnostic
procedures unless the astrologer is also licensed to
practice medicine. A skilled astrologer can identify
from the natal chart deficiences that cause disease and
then suggest medical tests to confirm the diagnosis.
Few physicians and psychiatrists are willing to work
with an astrologer; those who do find the service
invaluable, especially for cases in which causative
factors are hidden or disguised.
The medical astrologer works from the premise that
illness is a result of the misuse or misdirection of
planetary energies and that the square, quincunx and
opposition describe deficiencies in the human body
that may leave one vulnerable to disease. An illness
indicated in the birth chart manifests when progressed
and/or transiting planets trigger the natal potential.
Once inherent lacks are identified, treatment is directed
toward cause rather than symptoms.
The techniques of medical astrology can also be
successfully applied to preventive medicine. Helpful
immunization or prophylactic procedures can be
instituted to overcome body weaknesses described in
the natal chart. Also, some herbalists rely upon an
astrological assessment of body needs when
recommending natural remedies to combat disease or
to build up the body.
Modern medical astrology, still in its infancy,
demands a sophisticated approach. Studies conducted

others are being re-evaluated in light of current medical
and astrological thought. Much new research centers
around the nodal chart, midpoints, Uranian planets
and polarities in terms of medical correspondence. For
the interested astrologer who is willing to devote years
to advanced study, the field is wide open.
Mundane Astrology
Mundane astrology, unlike natal astrology, deals with
the world rather than the individual. Matters of political
significance to a particular nation or to the world as a
whole are part of this branch as are the weather,
revolutions, universal philosophical trends and current
events. The technical knowledge and advanced
techniques required in this highly specialized craft can
befound in literature devoted to thesubject. However,
something can be learned about national political and
philosophical developments by studying a horoscope
based on the "birthdate" of a country and adapting natal
symbolism to the nation instead of the individual.

Astrological Development:
Microcosm and Macrocosm
Astrological factors influence various phases of
individual human development, common generational
attributes and conditions that prevail over thousands
of years. They describe the psychological emphasis of
the particular period in life, generation or astrological
era with which they are associated. Although personal
growth (psychological, emotional, physical and
spiritual) varies with each individual, human
development follows a general pattern from birth
onward that is described by planets, which govern
each period of life.
Planetary Ages: Keys
to Human Development
Analysis of the planetary rulers of each period in life
according to strength or weakness by sign, house and
aspect in the natal chart indicates the ease or difficulty
with which an individual can successfully complete
each stage of development. Some people seem to be
"stuck" in a phase long after the corresponding
planetary age has ended; others advance much faster.
Knowledge of a client's developmental process enables
the astrologer to gear counseling within the frame of
current development and to help that person advance
to the next stage.
Traditionally, human life was thought to consist of
seven stages. However, in view of current longevity
and recognition of the spiritual aspects of human
nature as opposed to the purely physical (mental,
emotional and material body), Uranus, Neptune and
Pluto, which are not included in the traditional "seven
ages of man," are given rulership over specific periods
in life and afterlife along with the other seven planets
as noted in Chapter 3.
One cannot gain proper perspective by studying
only the planet associated with the year of interest.
A person's growth in each phase of life influences
development in following periods. For example, the
first seven years of life, ruled by the Moon, indicate
development of instinctive reactions. Reasoning is not
yet a tool available to the individual; the child learns
by copying the actions of other persons. If the Moon
is very strong natally by sign, house and aspect, this
person, as an adult, will tend to revert to action
without thought; reaction is emotional and instinctive
rather than logical. One may teach himself or herself
to stop and think in adult years, but the first and
strongest instinct will be to respond emotionally.
Mercury, ruler of years seven to fifteen, brings into
play the ability to think and plan action through
rational thought. This period, one of primary learning,
focuses on education and communication with others.
A strong natal Mercury indicates that the individual
will be guided in later years by rational thought rather
than emotions. Mercury retrograde in the natal chart
shows a tendency to internalize intellectual processes.
Since Mercury's retrograde period averages about three
weeks, progressed Mercury will go direct within the first
twenty-one years of life. At this juncture, great change
in the use of communicative and thought processes
occurs as intellectual development becomes
externalized. An afflicted Mercury does not necessarily
indicate difficulty in grasping ideas but it can mean
the individual has trouble communicating them and
moving into the next stage of development

Attracting others, love, art and beauty are important

possessions and relationships become meaningful. The
strength or weakness of natal Venus indicates how the
individual will incorporate Venus principles in
succeeding periods of life. With positive development
during this stage, art, love and beauty can become
primary motivations throughout life. If negative
attributes develop, the individual may never be satisfied
with relationships or material assets; the inner need for
beauty and art may be stifled or unfulfilled.
The years of self-discovery, creativity and

can develop. This is a crucial period in psychological
and personal growth, for it represents the "I of life,"

The energy years, from ages thirty-four to forty-
five, are ruled by Mars. During this period one asserts
himself or herself in the world in an attempt to find
a direction to life and career. Mars rules desires, and
the Mars years are dedicated to fulfilling desires.
Positive development indicates commitment to goals
and facilitates success. Negative expression manifests
in frustration, anger, and in some cases, violence.
Mars energy, if not developed constructively, becomes
self-destructive.
Jupiter governs ages forty-five to fifty-seven, the

expressed during the Mars phase of development. The
Jupiter years can be disappointing if one failed to find

Opportunities, usually most abundant at this stage,

Satum, traditionally associated with the final stage

reckoning. The rewards and recognition one has
earned now manifest. If previous phases have not been
utilized in a positive way, recognition and acclaim may

Uranus years, ages seventy to eighty-four, are years
of change, change that can manifest in an unexpected
and often erratic manner. Some people adjust well to
this period during which responsibilities of former
years no longer exist and develop more fully along
spiritual and creative lines; others do not. These years
can mark a period of inner awakening, spiritual
growth and purpose, a time when one utilizes life's
experiences and directs knowledge and energy toward
making the world a better place in which to live. For
those who fail to respond to higher Uranian vibrations,
growth may be interrupted or distorted. Unpredictable

previous stages of development are incomplete.
Neptune rules ages eighty-four to ninety-nine when

Pluto, associated with the period from one hundred

reincarnation. At this stage of development, the body
is no longer a prime focus; the responsibilities and
experiences of life have been accomplished or at least

One's growth pattern is not fatalistic; it can be changed

Influenced by the Outermost Planets

generational developments. As one or another of these
planets changes sign, differences within the same
generation become apparent and misunderstandings
between the young and the old are created. Motivation
and action of a generation differ according to changes
in the mode and element of predominating signs. For
example, a shift from a cardinal to a fixed sign (mode)
or fire to earth (element) brings about a corresponding
shift in generational emphasis.

as we now know it, drastic steps will probably be
undertaken. If action is geared to positive planetary
and sign influence, useful government reforms can be
instituted, nuclear hazards controlled and pollution
problems resolved. If negative action predominates,
nuclear accidents and pollution poisoning on a world-

years mark a turning point in world history is evident
with two planets operating in Capricorn, the sign
associated with governments and their activities, and
Pluto, the planet that rules evolution and trans-
formation, operating in its own sign, Scorpio.
A world-wide spiritual regeneration will probably
follow on the heels of the governmental shake-up that
may occur in the nineties as Pluto enters Sagittarius
in 1995. This century closes and a new age begins with
both Uranus (1995/96) and Neptune (1998/99) in

based on compassion will be the driving force for this

for all humankind. Fittingly, Uranus, which rules

associated with the occult in Sagittarius, ruler of the

promises learning, discovery and expansion associated
with astrology.
Astrological Eras: The Great Year
The emphasis of an astrological era, a period of
approximately two thousand years equal to one Great
Year month, is reflected in characteristics common to
different cultures during the period. The duration of
a Great Year depends upon the motion of Earth's pole.
Uneven effects of the gravitational pull of the Sun and
Moon on Earth's equator create nutation (from the
Latin nutare, to nod), a small nodding motion or
wobble in Earth's axis. As a result, the poles of Earth's
axis slowly revolve around the pole of the ecliptic,
taking approximately 25,800 calendar years to
complete a circle (cycle), one Great Year.
This complex motion influences the direction in
which Earth's pole points (now toward Polaris, the
North Star, in a few thousand years toward Alpha
Cephei, the future Polestar) and Precession of the

=== Page 234 ===
Astrological Development: Microcosm and Macrocosm 261
Equinoxes (refer to Chapter 1). The vernal equinoctial
point (0° Aries) moves such that a different
constellation appears as its celestial backdrop every
two thousand years or so depending upon the size of
the constellation since some are larger than others.
Relative motion between the equinoctial point and the
constellations is backward, proceeding from the end
to the beginning of a constellation, so changing
background constellations appear in reverse zodiacal
order. A Great Year is divided into twelve "months"
(astrological eras), each ruled by the sign that
corresponds to the constellation forming the backdrop
for 0° Aries during that period.
The sign associated with an astrological era and its
planetary ruler exert broad influence on world affairs
and cultures during the period. It is difficult to
determine exact significance in early eras before history
was recorded; however, artifacts and religious legends
associated with various historical periods do relate to
corresponding astrological eras.
During the early Mesolithic Period (Pre-Neolithic),
which began ca, 12,000 B.C., primitives started to
domesticate animals and build crude shelters, both
Virgo functions. In about two thousand years, these
peoples had progressed to the point that religion
became more complex and they developed elaborate
burial rites, an attribute of Leo. In some regions,
cremation of the dead (Leo is a fire sign) was practiced.
Further evidence that Leo and its ruler, the Sun, played

discovery of religious artifacts believed to be symbols
of the Sun.
The great floods that appeared in all parts of Earth

A flood legend is part of the tradition of most early
cultures, and various written sources, including the
Epic of Cilgamesh from the ancient Babylonians and
the Old Testament, refer to a great deluge that
destroyed all living things not protected by theirgod
This period also gave rise to Moon worship, cults
devoted to goddesses and fertility rites.
At about the time the Neolithic Period opened, the
age of Gemini (ca. 6,000 B.C.) began. It was during

People became more militant under the influence

Many cultures adopted warlike gods, heroes for whom
they fought and conquered. This was the age of the

introduced the Iron Age about 1,100 B.C., and the

The present astrological era, the age of Pisces, began

Planetary Nodes and Solstice Points
Planetary nodes and solstice points, sensitive points
in a horoscope once disregarded by many natal
astrologers, are fast becoming topics of concentrated
study and discussion. That they are significant to
astrology is generally accepted, but their exact
meaning and influence are still matters of conjecture
and controversy.
Planetary Nodes
The nodes of a planet are points in space at which the
plane of the planet's orbit intersects the plane of the
ecliptic. The zodiacal degree occupied by a planet when
its path crosses the ecliptic from south to north marks
the position of its north node (ascending node); the
position of its south node (descending node) depends on
its zodiacal position when it crosses the ecliptic from
north to south. A planet's crossing of the ecliptic is
indicated when its celestial latitude, the distance it lies
north or south of the ecliptic, is zero. The ecliptic is
defined by the Sun's apparent path; therefore, the Sun
cannot travel north or south relative to the ecliptic and
has no nodal points (refer to Chapter I).
The Moon's Nodes are an important part of
astrological theory and delineation. According to sign
and house, the position of the Moon's North Node in
the horoscope points out attitudes, actions and
interests that promote an individual's development;
its South Node is associated with tendencies that
inhibit growth (see Chapters 3, 4 and 7). The Moon's
Nodes also have a role in eclipses, the significance of
which is discussed in Chapter 10.
Because they are not so well understood, planetary
nodes are not given as much consideration as lunar
nodes. (It is customary to reserve the term planetary
nodes for nodes other than those of the Moon.)
Planetary nodes are listed in most astronomical tables
according to their heliocentric positions. Most
horoscopes are based on the geocentric positions of
planets and the Moon's Nodes (Chapter 1), It is
perplexing and somewhat absurd to relate a
heliocentric factor to a geocentric horoscope, so for
years planetary nodes have been ignored by many
astrologers.
It is not necessary to master intricate calculations
in order to determine the geocentric position of a
node if geocentric tables are unavailable. Many helio-
centric tables list the date on which a planet reaches
its nodal point; one can look up the planet's zodiacal
position in an ephemeris on that date to find the
approximate position of the node in geocentric terms.
Alternatively, one can determine from the ephemeris
the time and date on which a planet's celestial latitude
is 0°, note whether the planet is moving from south
to north or vice versa and record its zodiacal position
which is the nodal position at that time
The north and south nodes of planets, excluding the
Moon, do not necessarily lie opposite each other
geocentrically, although they do when measured in
the heliocentric system. The fundamental meaning of
nodes is based upon the polarity ot the north and south
node and the axis that connects them Traditionally,
the functions ol a planet's north and south node are
interdependent. The north node is described as a
positive pole with a conscious function and the south

=== Page 238 ===
266 Compendium of Astrology
node as a negative pole with a subconscious function.
It is believed that the north node represents a point
of intake at which energy is focused and the south node
a point of release for that energy. Another view
attributes strength to a planet when it is at its north
node and weakness to its position at the south node.
However, if a geocentric pair of nodes are not in
polarity, traditional meanings are not applicable.
Perhaps the problem lies not in lack of polarity but
in failure to recognize that planetary nodes (as
distinguished from lunar nodes) do not bear the same
relationship to Earth as do the Moon's Nodes. The solar
orbit of the Moon, Earth's satellite, depends upon Earth's
orbit. This cannot be said of the planets. (Interplanetary
gravitational forces are not considered here.) Is it possible
that the point opposite a planet's geocentric north node,
designated here as the theoretical south node, indicates
a balance point through which the real south node must
operate in order for the full potential of the north node
to be realized? Accordingly, the natural tendency lies
with the real south node, which signifies a source of
disharmony or inherent weakness; correction of these
deficiencies rests with the theoretical south node. This
then suggests that the individual strive to achieve balance
by utilizing south node (real) lessons in the manner and
area indicated by the theoretical south node thus
establishing effective polarity, which permits the
theoretical south node to act as the channel for release
and dispersion of energies introduced at the north node.
A more logical assumption makes it unnecessary to
devise an imaginary node. The fact that a pair of
planetary nodes does not lie in exact opposition may be
a fundamental factor that has been overlooked in
interpreting nodes. Perhaps planetary nodes are not
analogous to lunar nodes. The distortion of the nodal
axis may be meaningful in itself. If a planet's nodes do
not lie at opposite poles of a nodal axis, polarity and
complementarity are destroyed. Input at the north node
fails to be released or utilized at the south node. The
south node then takes on the character of an obstruction
(psychological or physical) that interferes with planetary
action as well as receptivity of the north node. The "kink"
in the nodal axis is descriptive of a perturbation that
creates turmoil (eased or reinforced by aspects to the
nodes) in areas of nodal and planetary influence, turmoil
that is "circular" in nature. Thus a planet's influence is
felt at its nodal points; the nodal points and aspects to
them affect planetary development.
For instance, psychologically-based fears or
prejudices, or material circumstances as described by
Mercury's south node, might explain interruptions in
intellectual development that are apparent in the
individual but not otherwise accounted for in the birth
chart. The key to reaching mental potentials indicated
by Mercury rest with recognizing and overcoming
south node obstructions. However, Mercury and its
nodes are interrelated in such a way that action at
either nodal point or by Mercury influences areas
designated by the other two points. Therefore,
improvement in areas governed by Mercury or
sensitized by its north node is helpful in dealing with
south node problems.
For example, assume that Mercury is in Capricorn in
the tenth house, its north node in Aquarius in the
eleventh house and its south node in Sagittarius in the
ninth house (a real geocentric possibility). Narrow
religious views or lack of higher education (south node
in Sagittarius in the ninth house) might interfere with
intellectual development (Mercury), career advance-
ment, one's position in society (Mercury in Capricorn
in the tenth house), humanitarian understanding and
interaction in social groups (north node in Aquarius in
the eleventh house). The key to advancement
intellectually, professionally and socially lies in higher
education or religious tolerance. Since action is circular,
improvement in any one area will have a positive effect
on the other two. That is, educational advancement can
help career standing and community position, give
insight into humanitarian causes and permit freer social
relationships. Conversely, education may be advanced
through professional interests (on-the-job training or
education at company expense) or through the
organizations to which one belongs.
The exact significance of planetary nodes will not
be determined until lengthy and detailed studies of case
histories are completed. However, at this point, it
seems probable that an approach that views the
three factors, a planet and both its nodes, as three
components of a single element, is valid.
Solstice Points
Although solstice points (antiscian or mirror points)
are more commonly used in horary than in natal
astrology, they are worth calculating and studying.
It is believed that they indicate turning points in life

=== Page 239 ===
Planetary Nodes and Solstice Points 267
that manifest when they are aspected by progressed
or transiting planets. It has been shown that a
progressed or transiting aspect to a solstice point
activates the planet to which that point relates. For
example, if progressed Sun conjuncts natal Mars'
solstice point, Sun/Mars activity manifests according
to a Sun/Mars conjunction even though progressed
Sun does not actually aspect natal Mars.
Solstice points are based on the fact that the Sun
occupies the same degree of declination at points
equidistant from 0° Cancer (summer solstice point) and
0° Capricorn (winter solstice point). For instance, the
Sun's declination when it is at 15° Taurus and at 15° Leo
is the same,- both zodiacal points are 45° from 0° Cancer
and 135° from 0° Capricorn. Therefore, the equidistant
points share a common relationship in respect to the
celestial equator on which declination is based.
To calculate the solstice point of a planet or angle,
subtract the degrees and minutes of its zodiacal position
from 29°60'; find the proper sign in the table below.

Fixed Stars
A planet or angle that falls within 1° orb of the position
of a fixed star is emphasized in the horoscope. The
strength a fixed star exerts in the horoscope depends upon
that star's magnitude or degree of brightness with
reference to Polaris (the polestar), a star of the second
magnitude. The brightest and most influential stars are
classed as first magnitude stars.
Thousands of stars are visible. The following list
contains twenty-six fixed stars commonly used in
astrology. The positions of the stars listed were correct
for 1980. To find the zodiacal longitude for any other
year, multiply the number of years between 1980 and
the year of interest by 50.25. The result is the required
correction in seconds of longitude. If the year of interest
is earlier than 1980, subtract the correction from the 1980
position. If the given year is later than 1980, add the
correction to the listed position. For example, to find the
position of a fixed star in 1945, multiply 35 (1980 — 1945
= 35) by 50,25. The result is 1,759 seconds of longitude,
which converts to 29' 19". Subtract this correction from
the 1980 position.
Astrologers are not in agreement as to the
significance of fixed stars in a natal horoscope. Some
astrologers do not consider fixed star influence in their
analyses. Each fixed star is thought to express
attributes similar to those of one or more of the
planets. Some fixed stars carry negative connotations,
others positive. A few display both benefic and malefic
properties. As a general rule a fixed star reinforces
those qualities of the planet or angle it conjuncts that
most closely match its own nature and those of the
planet(s) that it resembles.

^ ^Arabian Parts
Other than the Part of Fortune (Chapter 13), Arabian
Parts (or Points) are not much used in modern
astrology. The system of combining three points of
a horoscope to form a particular "part" regarded as
a sensitive point was developed in Arabia during the
Middle Ages. Since then, additional "Arabian" Parts
have been devised.
Certain of the parts show by house placement
in the natal chart the house a related planet occupies
in a solar chart, a chart whose first house cusp is
at the Sun's zodiacal position (Chapter 12). Thus, by
using these parts, one can compare solar house
emphasis with natal house emphasis without erecting
a solar chart.
For example, if the Part of Fortune, which is
calculated by adding the positions of the Ascendant
and Moon and subtracting the Sun's position from the
sum, is in the ninth house of a natal chart, the Moon
occupies the ninth house in that person's solar chart.
Other parts that relate similarly to a solar chart are
calculated as follows:
Part of Commerce (Caduceusl: Ascendant plus
Mercury minus the Sun. The Caduceus indicates the
solar house of Mercury.
Part of Love (Heart): Ascendant plus Venus minus the
Sun. The heart indicates the solar house of Venus.
Part of Passion (Sword): Ascendant plus Mars
minus the Sun. The Sword indicates the solar house
of Mars.
Part of Increase (Pomegranate): Ascendant plus Jupiter
minus the Sun. The Pomegranate indicates the solar
house of Jupiter.
Part of Fate (Hourglass): Ascendant plus Satum minus
the Sun. The Hourglass indicates the solar house of
Saturn. It is sometimes called the Part of
Responsibility.
Part of Catastrophe (Lightning Flash): Ascendant plus
Uranus minus the Sun. The Lightning Flash indicates
the solar house of Uranus,
Part of Treachery (Trident): Ascendant plus Neptune
minus the Sun. The trident indicates the solar house
of Neptune.
Part of Organization (Gavel): Ascendant plus Pluto
minus the Sun. The Gavel indicates Pluto's solar house
position.
The names of the parts are symbolic of their
meanings. When aspected natally or by progression,
the parts illuminate conditions with which they are
associated. For instance, aspects to the Heart (Part of
Love) describe conditions that affect love and
affectional relationships in context with the rest of the
horoscope. Parts that do not relate to the solar chart
in the same manner as the above include the following:
Part of Spirit: Ascendant plus Sun minus the Moon.
Part of Faith: Ascendant plus Mercury minus the Moon.
Part of Female Children. Ascendant plus Venus minus
the Moon.
Part of Male Children: Ascendant plus Jupiter minus
the Moon.
Part of Death: Ascendant plus cusp of the eighth house
minus the Moon. This part is read in conjunction with
the Anareta.

Apheta, also Alphela Literally, the giver of life. A well

co-ruler Prior to the discovery of Uranus, the Sun
and Moon were believed to rule one sign each
and the other five planets then known to
humankind (Mercury through Saturn) to rule
two signs each. When the three outermost
planets were discovered, they became co-rulers
of the signs Aquarius (Uranus), Pisces (Neptune)
and Scorpio (Pluto), along with the traditional
rulers Saturn, Jupiter and Mars respectively.
Modern studies seem to indicate that the new
co-rulers are primary rulers of the signs with
which they are associated and may be sole
rulers, in which case, two other planets, one
linked to Libra (or Taurus) and the other to
Virgo, may await discovery, thus eliminating
dual rulership.
Co-rulership of a house is shared by planets

grand cross, grand square An aspect configuration in
which four planets, each in a different sign of the
same quadruplicity, form mutual squares. Much
tension is generated among planets forming this
pattern. If signs are mixed (aspects within orb but
not in signs of the same quadruplicity), the
impact associated with a grand square is
somewhat diminished,
grand trine The aspect pattern formed when three
planets, each in a different sign of the same
triplicity (air, earth, fire or water), trine each
other. A grand trine permits smooth flow of
energies among the planets involved in
accordance with the triplicity occupied. A
dissociate grand trine, one in which the three
planets fall within orb to form mutual trines but
do not occupy the same triplicity, supplements
ease of planetary expression but lacks the
cohesiveness of a grand trine formed between
planets occupying one triplicity.
great circle A circle described on the surface of a
sphere (Earth, for example) so that its plane
passes through the center of the sphere.
Great Year The astrological era based on the time it
takes Earth's axis to complete one revolution
around the pole of the ecliptic, about twenty-five
thousand years. A Great Year is divided into
twelve "months" of about two thousand years
duration. See also precession.
Greater Benefic A term reserved for the planet Jupiter
which, according to ancient beliefs, was
responsible for life's greatest blessings.
Greater Malefic A term applied to Satum, the planet
ancients believed to generate the evils in life.
Gregorian calendar The calendar now used
internationally, devised by Pope Gregory in the
1580s to replace the Julian calendar, which by
then had accumulated a ten-day discrepancy
with the solar year. Most, but not all, countries
accepted the Pope's calendar by the 1700s (Great
Britain, 1752). Russia did not change until 1918
and Turkey in 1928. Astrologers working with
older dates should determine whether they are
based on the Julian calendar, designated Old
Style or OS, or on the Gregorian calendar,
designated New Style or NS.
Hades The second symbolic planet used in Uranian
astrology. See also Uranian astrology.
Halley's Comet Named for the English astronomer,
Edmund Halley, who correctly predicted, in
1682, the comet's return in 1759. One of the most
brilliant comets viewed from Earth, it reappears
approximately every seventy-seven years,
half-sum An alternate term for midpoint, the point
in the zodiac that lies exactly midway between
two planets.
hard aspects Aspects that stimulate action or tension
and induce motivation. All hard aspects are
disharmonious to some extent except the
conjunction and parallel, whose influence
depends largely upon the natures of the planets
involved; that is, planetary energies do not merge
smoothly when two planets form a hard aspect
such as the semi-square, square, opposition or
sesquiquadrate.
harmonics The term for zodiacal aspects that
describes the energy levels or vibrational
frequencies associated with aspects. An aspect,
derived from the division of a circle (360°) by a
whole number, and its multiples share the same
frequency and therefore operate at similar energy
levels. For example, division of 360° by four
yields 90°, a square. The square is a fourth
harmonic aspect as are its multiples, 180°
(opposition) and 270°. Several harmonics may
merge in a single aspect. The square is a multiple
of the semisquare (45°), an eighth harmonic
aspect; the square's primary harmonic is four
(sometimes written 1/4) and its sub-harmonic is
eight (2/8, second of the eighth harmonic). The
opposition's primary harmonic is two (1/2 X
360° = 180°); its sub-harmonics are four (2/4,
second in the series of fourth harmonics), six
(3/6, third of the sixth harmonic), eight (4/8,
fourth of the eighth harmonic), etc.
harmonious aspects Aspects in which the planets
involved are mutually supportive; their energies
operate together comfortably and productively.
The sextile and trine are major harmonious
aspects; also called easy aspects,
heliocentric Measurements based upon the Sun as the
central point of reference or observation; Sun-
centered.
Herschel The original name for the planet Uranus,
which was discovered in 1781 by the British
astronomer Sir William Herschel.

logarithm From the Latin logarithmus, literally

the larger units (hours to minutes of time or

seconds of time),

Precession of the Equinoxes The gradual westward

movement of the poles of Earth's axis. This

radical Having to do with the natal horoscope,
radical chart The natal horoscope. In horary astrology,
the term radical applies to achartdeemed readable
by virtue of the Ascendant being greater than 3°
and less than 27° in any sign,
radical position The position a planet occupies in a
natal horoscope,
radix From theLatin, literally root. A natal horoscope,
rapport measurement From the French, literally
related measurement: applied to progressions
based on advancing a planet's natal position one
degree for each year after birth,
reception Shortened form of mutual reception. See
mutual reception,
rectification The correcting of an inexact birthtime
or the determining of an unknown birthtime
through astrological methods,
refranation The failure of an applying aspect to
culminate, when the significator turns
retrograde before reaching partile.
Regiomontanus The German astrologer (fifteenth
century) who devised the house system that
bears his name. This system is based upon
twelve equal divisions along Earth's equator
projected upon the ecliptic,
relative houses Houses three, seven, and eleven,
ruled naturally by air signs. Function focuses
on human relationships. As a group, these
houses form the Trinity of Association,
retrograde application Term used in reference to a
retrograde planet which, because of its retrograde
motion, applies to an aspect with another planet.
If both planets are moving toward each other, the
term mutual application is used,
retrograde motion The apparent backward motion
of a planet when it appears, as observed from
Earth, to reverse its natural direction of travel
and move backward in the zodiac,
revolution One complete orbit or cycle. In a natal
chart, a planet s return to its natal degree upon
completing a circuit of the map.
right ascension Measurement along the celestial
equator eastward from 0° Aries that describes
planetary positions in terms of degrees, minutes
and seconds, not zodiacal signs. Sidereal time
expressed in unit of arc.
rising sign Synonymous with Ascendant, Sec
Ascendant.
ruminant signs An obsolete term applied to signs
symbolized by cud-chewing animals, namely,
Aries (ram), Taurus (bull) and Capricorn (goat).
Sabian symbols A system developed by Elsie VVheeler
(psychically). Marc Edmund lones and Dane
Rudhyar that assigns an occult or esoteric meaning
to each degree of the zodiac.
Saros cycle The eighteen-year (approximate) cycle
containing an average of forty-one solar eclipses
and twenty-nine lunar eclipses, in which an
eclipse from each current Saros Series appears,
satellitium A little-used term synonymous with
stellium. See ii/so multiple conjunction stellium.
secondary progressions, secondary directions The
method of progressing a natal horoscope in which
each day afterbirth is equated to a corresponding

=== Page 260 ===
290 Compendium of Astrology
number of years after birth; commonly referred
to as "day for a year" progressions.
See-Saw The shaping arrangement in which, according
to Marc Edmund Jones, the planets form two
distinct groups roughly opposite each other in a
horoscope; symbolizing balance or the need to
seek balance as a strong motivating factor,
semi-dedle The twentieth harmonic, 18°; interpreted
as a weak minor easy aspect. Also called a
vigintile.
semi-quintile See decile.
semi-sextile One of the more influential minor easy
aspects, the twelfth harmonic, 30°.
semi-square The eighth harmonic, 45°; an important
minor hard aspect in which planetary energies do
not merge harmoniously but produce friction,
separating aspect One in which the significator
(faster moving planet of the two in aspect) is
moving away from partile (the degree at which
the aspect is exact),
septile The seventh harmonic, 51 3/7°. A little-used
minor aspect, probably inharmonious, thought
to be associated with karma,
sesquiquadrate, sesqui-square A multiple of the semi-
square, and eighth harmonic aspect. A minor
hard aspect, separating distance 135°, its
influence is frictional.
sesquiquintile See tredecile.
sexdle The sixth harmonic, 60°; a major easy aspect
considered beneficial and opportune,
shaping Descriptive of the visual arrangement of
planets in a horoscope. Marc Edmund Jones iden-
tified seven different patterns; the Bowl, Bucket,
Bundle, Locomotive, See-Saw, Splash and Splay.
Each shaping type is linked to specific astrological
conditions and a particular interpretational focus.
See individual listings. Shaping is also referred to
as planetary pictures and planetary patterns. See
also planetary patterns,
short ascension Refers to the six signs that take less
time than the other six to rise above the horizon,
namely, Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Capricorn,
Aquarius and Pisces; the spring and winter signs
in the northern hemisphere. See also long
ascension.
sidereal astrology An astrological system based upon
the constellations, not the tropical zodiac,
sidereal day Twenty-four sidereal hours equal to 23
hours, 56 minutes and 4 seconds of clock time.
sidereal time Time measured in relation to fixed stars,
as distinguished from clock time, based upon the
Sun's position relative to Earth. Astrological time
data is listed in sidereal time units,
sidereal zodiac Based on the division of the circle of
twelve constellations: Aries, Taurus, Gemini,
Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius,
Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces; the basis for
sidereal astrology,
significator The faster moving of two planets in
aspect; the significator is said to aspect the
slower moving planet (promittor). Also used in
reference to the planetary ruler of a house,
matter, object or person. See also promittor.
singleton A planet that is the sole occupant of the
horoscope hemisphere in which it is placed; said
to give balance to a horoscope that has nine
planets in the other hemisphere. See also Bucket,
signs The twelve divisions of the zodiac: Aries, T aurus,
Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio,
Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius and Pisces,
sinister aspect From the Latin sinister, left or left
hand; a term replaced by modern astrologers
with departing aspect, which refers to aspects
in which the direction from significator to
promittor is backward in the zodiac, clockwise
in a horoscope. See also departing aspect,
slow of course Term used to describe a planet's
motion when its rate of travel is less than its
mean daily motion,
solar From the Latin sol, the Sun; refers to the Sun.
solar arc The distance the Sun travels from birth
position to its secondary progressed position.
A system of progressions adds the solar arc at
a given year to the natal positions of house cusps
and/or planets. A similar method based on the
mean solar arc multiplies 59' 08" (Naibod arc,
Sun's mean daily motion) by the individual's age
in years to determine the proper increment to
add to natal positions,
solar eclipse See eclipse.
solar return, solar revolution A horoscope erected
for the exact time in a given year when the
transiting Sun reaches the same position it held
in the natal horoscope; used to project
conditions for the year of interest,
solstice Either of two points on the ecliptic at which
the Sun reaches its farthest point north (0°
Cancer) or south (0° Capricorn) of the equator.

=== Page 261 ===
Glossaru 291
The longest day of the year occurs at summer
solstice (first day of summer) as the Sun moves
at its slowest rate; the winter solstice marks the
shortest day of the year as the Sun reaches its
fastest rate of travel.
Splash A planetary arrangement described by Marc
Edmund Jones in which the planets are fairly
evenly distributed around the horoscope. This
dispersion of planets suggest dispersion of
interests.
Splay A planetary arrangement identified by lack of
symmetry and irregularly spaced planets and
groups of planets as described by Marc Edmund
Jones: symbolic of individualism and
nonconformity,
square Fourth harmonic, 90°. A major hard aspect,
the square generates tension and stirs action.
Also called a quadrate, quartile or tetragon,
station A planet is said to "make a station" at the
degree it occupies when it appears motionless
as its direction changes from direct to retrograde
or vice versa,
stationary, stationary motion Term used to describe
apparent lack of motion when a planet's
direction of travel changes from direct (forward
in the zodiac) to retrograde (backward in the
zodiac) or vice versa. Planetary energy, focused
at the stationary position, is considered strong
in a horoscope when a planet is stationary,
stellium A multiple conjunction that occurs within one
sign or house, indicating a focal point of energy
orinterest. Also called a satellitium. The term may
include multiple conjunctions that occupy more
than one sign. See also multiple conjunction,
succedent houses From the L^tin succedere, to follow;
houses two, five, eight and eleven, which follow
the angular houses. Also called fixed houses, being
ruled naturally by the fixed signs: Taurus, Leo,
Scorpio and Aquarius. The mode of action
associated with these houses reflects fixed qualities
of steadiness and reliability,
superior planets Planets whose orbits are larger than
Earth's. The term is sometimes restricted to the
three outermost planets: Uranus, Neptune and
Pluto.
swift in motion Said of a planet whose rate of travel
is greater than its mean daily motion,
synastry The astrological technique of comparing
natal horoscopes to gain insight into the
strengths and weaknesses inherent in the rela-
tionship that exists between the individuals
involved. See also composite chart,
synodic Refers to the period between two successive
conjunctions formed by the same two planets,
syzygy From the Latin, yoked together: refers to
points at which a planet conjuncts or opposes
the Sun; usually used in reference to those
Sun/Moon conjunctions and oppositions that
are eclipse events.
Table of Houses An astrological reference table,
correlated with a particular house system, which
lists the zodiacal positions of house cusps at
various latitudes according to sidereal time.
T-cross See T-square.
temporal houses Houses two, six and ten, ruled by
earth signs; symbolic of the material aspects of
life. As a group they form the Trinity of Wealth,
terrestrial Of the Earth, Earth-related,
terminal houses Those houses ruled naturally by
water signs: four, eight and twelve. They pertain
to endings and results and symbolize occult
interests. Collectively, they are known as the
Trinity of Psychism.
Tetrabiblos Ptolemy's four-volume treatise on astrol-
ogy (second century). See also Ptolemy, Claudius,
tetragon An alternate term for the square aspect. See
square.
transit The position and movement of a planet on a
given day; used in reference to planets that pass
over or aspect a natal planet or cross a natal house,
translation of light A term used in horary astrology
to describe the activity of a planet that applies in
aspect, in tum, to two other planets that are
separating from a mutual aspect, thereby trans-
lating 'light'' or energy and symbolically reuniting
the planets and the matters they represent,
tredecile, trecile A minor easy aspect belonging to
the tenth harmonic (decile) group; separating
distance 108°. Also called a sesquiquintile.
trigon The three member signs of a triplicity. Also
used as an alternate term for grand trine. Sec
also grand trine, triplicity.
trine The third harmonic, 120°; the most influential
major easy aspect. The trine blends planetary
energies, harmoniously indicating ease of
expression.
triplicity A group ol three signs belonging to the
same element: fire (Aries, Leo, Sagittarius)

=== Page 262 ===
292 Compendium of Astrology
earth (Taurus, Virgo, Capricorn), air (Gemini,
Libra, Aquarius) and water (Cancer, Scorpio,
Pisces). The members of a triplicity lie 120°
apart in the zodiac, forming a trigonal and
harmonious relationship with each other,
tri-septile A seldom-used minor aspect, probably
inharmonious, belonging to the septile (seventh
harmonic) family; separating distance, 154017'.
tropical signs Cancer and Capricorn; so-called because
they occupy parts of the ecliptic where the Sun
reaches its farthest point north (Tropic of Cancer)
and south (Tropic of Capricorn). The Sun's
ingress into these signs marks the summer and
winter solstices respectively. See also solstice,
tropical zodiac The circle of signs that follows the
apparent path of the Sun (ecliptic). Also called
the movable zodiac because it shifts slightly each
year relative to the constellations of the sidereal
zodiac. See also Precession of the Equinoxes.
T-square The aspect pattern formed when two planets
in opposition both square the same third planet,
which acts a focal point for planetary energies,
under the Sunbeams Said of a planet that is within
17° of the Sun but out of conjunction orb.
universal time Greenwich Mean Time.
Uranian astrology A school of astrology, founded
by Alfred Witte in Hamburg, Germany, which
relies heavily upon the interpretational emphasis
of midpoints. In addition to traditional
astrological elements, it includes as symbolic
indicators eight hypothetical planets; Cupido,
Hades, Zeus, Kronos, Apollon, Admetos,
Vulkanus and Poseidon,
vernal From the Latin vemus, belonging to spring;
of or pertaining to spring. See also equinox.
Vertex The point found in the western section of a
horoscope that indicates the intersection of the
ecliptic and prime vertical, called the "third
angle of a horoscope." This point and its
opposite, the Anti-Vertex, are sensitive degrees
in a natal horoscope associated with fate and
wish fulfillment.
Vesta The fourth asteroid of astrological interest
discovered in the early nineteenth century.
Named after the virgin fire goddess (Roman),
its symbolic influence is protective.
Via Combusta Literally fiery way; refers to a section
of fixed stars that falls between 15° Libra and 15°
Scorpio. Used primarily in horary astrology as an
indication of unfortunate or ineffectual situations,
vigintile Alternate term for semi-decile. See semi-
decile.
vocational astrology That branch of astrology devoted
to career counseling in terms of the aptitudes and
needs shown in the natal horoscope,
void of course A term describing a planet that does
not apply to a major aspect until it changes sign,
usually confined to reference to the Moon. In
horary astrology, a void-of-course Moon indi-
cates lack of action or dynamics.
Vulcan A hypothetical planet whose orbit is said to
lie between Mercury and the Sun, about twelve
million miles from the Sun. Astronomers have
no evidence of this planet as yet.
Vulkanus The seventh symbolic planet used in
Uranian astrology. See also Uranian astrology,
waning That phase of the lunation cycle from full
Moon (Sun/Moon opposition) to new Moon
(Sun/Moon conjunction) during which the
visible portion of the Moon decreases,
water signs Cancer, Scorpio and Pisces, members of
the water triplicity that symbolize receptivity,
sensitivity and emotional depth,
waxing The phase of the lunation cycle from new
Moon (Sun/Moon conjunction) to full
(Sun/Moon opposition) during which the Moon
appears to grow larger, increasing in light,
yod An aspect configuration in which two planets in
sextile both form a quincunx (inconjunct) with the
same third planet; it is given a karmic
connotation. Sometimes called the Fingerof God.
zenith The point in the celestial sphere directly
overhead; opposite the nadir. The zenith and
nadir are the poles of the horizon.
Zeus The third symbolic planet used in Uranian
astrology. See also Uranian astrology,
zodiac From the Greek zodiakos, literally circle of
animals. See also tropical zodiac, sidereal zodiac,
zodiacal aspects Aspects based upon planets'
zodiacal longitude as distinguished from
parallels and contraparallels, which depend
upon declination.
